articles.title: Russell Brand found guilty of rape and sexual assaults; actor being investigated over more rape allegations
articles.summary: A jury found the actor guilty on one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.
articles.body:
A jury in London found comedian and actor Russell Brand guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

The actor had been charged on seven counts: three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault, and one count of attempted indecent assault.

Following Thursday's verdict, London's Metropolitan Police Service told Yahoo News that Brand, 51, was facing further allegations of rape from two women.

"The suspect has previously been interviewed under caution in connection with the allegations," the force said in a statement. Brand has not been charged in relation to these claims.

Following a four-week trial at Southwark Crown Court in London, the jury found Brand guilty on four of the charges. He was acquitted of two rape counts and one count of attempted indecent assault.

He is due to be sentenced at Southwark Crown Court on Monday, Nov. 9. The judge said he should expect a lengthy prison term.

Brand became a household name in the U.K. in the 2000s as a comedian and broadcaster. He went on to star in the movies Get Him to the Greek in 2010 and Arthur the following year.

He married singer Katy Perry in October 2010, but Brand filed for divorce in December 2011, citing irreconcilable differences. Their divorce was finalized in July 2012.

The claims against Brand were made by six different women, spanning from 1999 to 2009. None of the women knew each other, but all of them came forward to police following a TV documentary and press reports in 2023, in which anonymous allegations were made by other women.

During the trial, the court heard tearful and forceful testimony from the six complainants, who are all entitled to lifelong anonymity.

The convictions included a rape that took place in 2009, involving a victim who went to Brand's home after meeting him at one of his gigs. She said she had engaged in consensual sex, but that Brand then raped her and removed a condom in the process.

Brand was also convicted of sexually assaulting a woman when he grabbed her breasts at a London bar in 2004.

He was also found guilty over an incident in 2009, in which he demanded a woman give him a massage in front of two of his colleagues and then put his head in her groin.

A third complaint of sexual assault was upheld when Brand was found guilty of pushing a woman who worked at a radio station up against a wall and forcibly kissing her.

Brand denied the charges and said he had never forced anyone to do something against their will.

CCTV footage released by the Metropolitan Police shows Brand being interviewed by police in custody in December 2023.

"As I've repeatedly stated publicly and written about extensively, I led a very promiscuous life in the past, which I've spent years openly denouncing," Brand can be seen saying. "I've never engaged in non-consensual sexual activity."

He said he did "not recall the names" of the complainants, or meeting them, adding, "However, it's entirely possible that I may have encountered them and we may have engaged in consensual sexual activity or physical contact that's been since reimagined."

Following the verdict, the judge told Brand he would be remanded in custody.

"You've been convicted of a number of offenses including rape," judge Joel Bennathan said. "The consequence of that is inevitably a significant custodial term. My current view is that I therefore have to remand you into custody."

In a statement, Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy, from London's Metropolitan Police Service, said: "Today's verdict is first and foremost a testament to the extraordinary courage, resilience and determination of the women who came forward and reported what happened to them."

The statement added: "Brand used his influence, status and fame to exploit and sexually offend against women.

"As his profile grew, so too did his sense of entitlement. I hope this conviction sends a clear message that no one is above the law, no matter how famous or powerful they may be."

Ron Brand, Russell's father, told the BBC he was "shocked" by the verdicts. "I just didn't expect this - it's wrong," he said. "It's devastating."

Russell Brand was accompanied by his wife, Laura, during the trial. (Neil Mockford via Getty Images)

articles.title: Frio deve voltar ao Centro-Sul após sequência de temporais | G1
articles.standfirst: Nova frente fria deve provocar chuva forte, rajadas de vento e risco de granizo no Sul e Sudeste neste sábado (7). A partir de domingo (8), temperaturas podem cair com a chegada do ar polar.
articles.summary: Nova frente fria deve provocar chuva forte, rajadas de vento e risco de granizo no Sul e Sudeste neste sábado (7). A partir de domingo (8), temperaturas podem cair.
articles.body:
Foto: RENATO S. CERQUEIRA/FUTURA PRESS/ESTADÃO CONTEÚDO

Depois dos temporais que atingiram o Sul do Brasil nesta semana, uma nova frente fria deve avançar pela região no sábado (7), aumentando novamente o risco de chuva forte, rajadas de vento e granizo em parte do Centro-Sul do país.

A mudança deve ocorrer após uma sexta-feira (6) de tempo mais firme em boa parte do Rio Grande do Sul e de Santa Catarina.

No Paraná, porém, a chuva ainda pode ocorrer em diferentes momentos do dia, principalmente nas regiões oeste, noroeste e norte do estado.

Segundo o Instituto Nacional de Meteorologia ( Inmet ), a aproximação dessa nova frente fria, associada à atuação de áreas de baixa pressão atmosférica, deve favorecer a formação de nuvens carregadas entre o Sul, o Centro-Oeste e o Sudeste durante o fim de semana.

A partir de domingo (8), a entrada de uma massa de ar polar também pode provocar queda acentuada das temperaturas, principalmente no Sul e em áreas do Sudeste.

🌧️ ENTENDA: Uma frente fria é a faixa de encontro entre uma massa de ar mais frio e outra de ar mais quente. Seu avanço pode favorecer a formação de nuvens carregadas, provocar temporais e reduzir as temperaturas após a passagem do sistema.

No Sul, esta sexta-feira deve começar com predomínio de sol em grande parte do Rio Grande do Sul. As temperaturas podem subir durante a tarde, principalmente no centro e oeste do estado, onde as máximas devem alcançar os 30°C em algumas cidades.

Em Santa Catarina, o tempo também tende a ficar mais firme durante boa parte do dia, mas há possibilidade de chuva moderada a forte a partir da tarde no oeste catarinense.

No Paraná, as pancadas podem atingir principalmente as regiões oeste, noroeste e norte, onde há risco de temporais isolados e acumulados elevados.

Em Curitiba (PR), a temperatura deve variar entre 15°C e 22°C nesta sexta-feira. Porto Alegre (RS) pode registrar mínima de 16°C e máxima de 29°C, sem previsão de chuva significativa na capital gaúcha.

No Sudeste, esta sexta-feira ainda deve ter pancadas de chuva em grande parte da região, embora o sol possa aparecer em alguns momentos.

Em São Paulo, a previsão é de chuva principalmente no oeste, noroeste e norte do estado, além de pancadas isoladas no litoral e no leste paulista.

O oeste do território paulista está entre as áreas com possibilidade de rajadas de vento de até 70 km/h.

Na capital, as temperaturas devem variar entre 18°C e 25°C, segundo a Climatempo. O dia pode começar com muitas nuvens e chuva durante a madrugada, mas há possibilidade de aberturas de sol à tarde.

No Rio de Janeiro (RJ), a máxima prevista é de 27°C, cerca de 8°C abaixo da temperatura registrada na quinta-feira (5).

Ainda há possibilidade de pancadas acompanhadas por trovoadas, principalmente durante a tarde, em diferentes áreas fluminenses.

Em Minas Gerais, os temporais devem atingir principalmente o Triângulo Mineiro, a Zona da Mata e áreas do centro e leste do estado.

Mapa mostra previsão de chuva para esta sexta (06/11) em todo o Brasil. — Foto: CPTEC/Inpe

Belo Horizonte (MG) aparece entre as cidades sob risco de pancadas fortes nesta sexta-feira.

No sábado, a chegada da nova frente fria deve aumentar o risco de temporais em São Paulo, principalmente no interior do estado, onde também há possibilidade de granizo.

A chuva pode atingir áreas do Triângulo Mineiro, do oeste e sul de Minas Gerais e do sul do Rio de Janeiro.

Apesar das pancadas, o calor deve aumentar em parte do Sudeste antes da entrada do ar frio. Em São Paulo (SP), a máxima pode chegar a 33°C no sábado, enquanto Belo Horizonte (MG) pode registrar 32°C e o Rio de Janeiro (RJ), 31°C.

A partir de domingo, a tendência é de queda das temperaturas em parte da região, associada à chegada do ar mais frio após a passagem da frente fria.

No Centro-Oeste, a chuva deve continuar entre sexta-feira e sábado, principalmente em Mato Grosso do Sul, Goiás e no Distrito Federal.

Na sexta-feira, há previsão de pancadas acompanhadas por trovoadas em diferentes áreas da região. Em Mato Grosso do Sul, o risco de temporais é maior no sudeste e no leste do estado, onde as rajadas de vento também podem alcançar 70 km/h.

Em Campo Grande (MS), os termômetros podem chegar aos 35°C, sob previsão de chuva e trovoadas à tarde e à noite.

Em Cuiabá (MT), o calor também deve continuar intenso, com máxima prevista de 39°C nesta sexta-feira.

No sábado, a chuva deve atingir principalmente o centro, sul e leste de Mato Grosso do Sul, além de Goiás, do Distrito Federal e do sudeste de Mato Grosso.

Temperaturas mínimas previstas para esta sexta (06/11) em todo o Brasil. — Foto: CPTEC/Reprodução

As pancadas podem ser fortes em alguns momentos, principalmente nas áreas próximas à faixa de atuação da nova frente fria.

No Nordeste, a previsão indica mais um fim de semana de calor intenso e baixa umidade relativa do ar em grande parte da região.

Na sexta-feira, os índices de umidade podem variar entre 12% e 20% no sul do Ceará, oeste de Pernambuco e norte da Bahia. Esses valores indicam condições de ar muito seco, principalmente durante as horas mais quentes da tarde.

O calor também deve continuar elevado. Em Teresina (PI), a máxima pode chegar a 40°C na sexta-feira e subir para 41°C no sábado.

Já no Norte, as pancadas devem continuar atingindo principalmente o oeste e centro do Amazonas, o Acre, Rondônia e Tocantins.

Na sexta-feira, as chuvas podem ser moderadas a fortes em parte do Amazonas e do Acre, principalmente durante os períodos de maior aquecimento.

No sábado, a previsão indica aumento da chuva no centro e sul do Tocantins, além de pancadas acompanhadas por trovoadas em áreas do Amazonas.

Em Roraima, no Amapá e no norte do Pará, a tendência é de tempo mais firme, com temperaturas elevadas.

articles.title: Consumo de carne de caça e comércio ilegal de animais silvestres persistem no Amazonas e em rotas de fronteira, aponta estudo | G1
articles.standfirst: Revisão científica inédita mapeou padrões, vetores e rotas do tráfico de fauna na Amazônia brasileira. O estado se destaca tanto pela relevância na conservação quanto pela vulnerabilidade em áreas de fronteira internacional.
articles.summary: Revisão científica inédita mapeou padrões, vetores e rotas do tráfico de fauna na Amazônia brasileira. O estado se destaca tanto pela relevância na conservação quanto pela vulnerabilidade em áreas de fronteira internacional.
articles.body:
Espécie resgatada de Gavião Pedrês — Foto: Divulgação

O tráfico de animais silvestres continua sendo um problema na Amazônia, impulsionado por diferentes formas de exploração da fauna, é o que revela o estudo "Human Ecology" . O levantamento reuniu dezenas de pesquisas para traçar as principais rotas do tráfico de fauna na Amazônia brasileira, apontando a tríplice fronteira com Colômbia e Peru como uma das zonas mais vulneráveis e críticas do estado.

Conforme apontam os pesquisadores no estudo, o comércio ilegal de fauna silvestre no bioma é impulsionado prioritariamente por quatro finalidades:

"diferente de outras regiões onde o foco do tráfico recua sobre aves ornamentais para cativeiro, na Amazônia a demanda por consumo consuntivo — especialmente de mamíferos de médio e grande porte, répteis e peixes — assume o protagonismo na dinâmica ilícita", diz um trecho do estudo.

O peso do Amazonas e a pressão sobre as espécies

No Amazonas, o uso alimentar da fauna silvestre está profundamente enraizado em contextos locais e culturais. Espécies frequentemente comercializadas em mercados públicos e feiras da região incluem:

Mamíferos: como a paca, a anta e o queixada.

Répteis e quelônios: como o jacaré-açu, a tartaruga-da-amazônia e o tracajá

Peixes ornamentais e de corte: com rotas internacionais expressivas que partem de rios amazonenses rumo a mercados globais.

Segundo os dados levantados pela pesquisa, cerca de 25,5% das espécies registradas nos comércios ilegais avaliados constam em listas oficiais de ameaça de extinção do ICMBio. Os autores ressaltam que "peixes e mamíferos de grande porte figuram entre os grupos mais vulneráveis à pressão da caça e da captura desregulada".

Filhotes de tracajás sendo devolvidos à natureza no Lago Babaçu, em Itacoatiara. — Foto: Liam Cavalcante/Rede Amazônica

O estudo detalha que o Amazonas integra zonas críticas de escoamento e transistores de fauna, com destaque para a região da tríplice fronteira entre Brasil, Colômbia e Peru.

Para os pesquisadores, essa área vulnerável atua como um corredor ativo para a circulação de subprodutos e animais silvestres, desafiando a fiscalização interestadual e internacional devido à vastidão territorial da bacia amazônica e à assimetria nas legislações de proteção entre os países vizinhos.

Outro ponto destacado pela investigação acadêmica é a sazonalidade ambiental.

Segundo a análise, durante a estação chuvosa, o volume de carne de caça comercializada tende a subir devido à menor disponibilidade ou dificuldade na pesca tradicional. Em contraponto, no período de seca, a descida dos rios facilita a captura de jacarés, a desova e a coleta de quelônios em praias fluviais, intensificando temporariamente a pressão sobre essas populações.

Desafios de fiscalização e alternativas sustentáveis

A pesquisa enfatiza que o combate ao comércio ilegal na Amazônia esbarra em barreiras logísticas severas e na escassez de recursos estruturais de fiscalização nos rios, portos, aeroportos e feiras livres.

Os autores também alertam que "o avanço do comércio clandestino para ambientes virtuais — como redes sociais, aplicativos de mensagens e plataformas digitais, tem tornado o monitoramento ainda mais complexo para os órgãos de segurança e meio ambiente".

Como recomendação final, o estudo reforça que políticas públicas eficazes não devem se apoiar apenas na repressão policial, mas na combinação de educação ambiental direcionada, melhoria de oportunidades socioeconômicas para populações vulneráveis e no fortalecimento de alternativas de manejo sustentável de base comunitária, a exemplo de iniciativas bem-sucedidas com o pirarucu, que demonstram ser possível aliar a conservação da biodiversidade à geração de renda na região.

articles.title: Prospera oferece serviços gratuitos em São Pedro da Aldeia neste sábado (07/11) | G1
articles.standfirst: Com mais de 100 voluntários, ação da Prolagos e do Instituto Aegea reúne atendimentos de saúde, cidadania, lazer e espaço para microempreendedores locais.
articles.summary: Com mais de 100 voluntários, ação da Prolagos e do Instituto Aegea reúne atendimentos de saúde, cidadania, lazer e espaço para microempreendedores locais.
articles.body:
Os serviços gratuitos fazem parte da programação que começará às 9h no CIEP 272, no bairro São João — Foto: Arquivo Prolagos

Consultas clínicas, exames de vista, atendimento odontológico, serviços de beleza, orientações sobre benefícios sociais e atividades para toda a família estarão disponíveis gratuitamente neste sábado (07/11), em São Pedro da Aldeia. A programação faz parte do Prospera – Um movimento pelo cuidado com a vida, iniciativa promovida pela Prolagos em parceria com o Instituto Aegea. O evento acontece das 9h às 13h, no CIEP 272 – Gabriel Joaquim dos Santos, na Estrada dos Passageiros, no bairro São João, e contará com a participação de mais de 100 voluntários, instituições parceiras e representantes do poder público.

A programação reúne, em um único espaço, atendimentos nas áreas de saúde, cidadania, bem-estar, educação e sustentabilidade.

Diversos serviços gratuitos na ação — Foto: Arquivo Prolagos

Entre os serviços confirmados estão consultas clínicas, mini check-up, exames de vista, atendimento odontológico, aferição de pressão arterial e glicose, orientações psicológicas e fisioterapêuticas, além de vacinação contra a influenza e vacinação antirrábica para cães. O público também poderá aproveitar serviços de beleza e autocuidado, como corte de cabelo, limpeza de pele e massagens corporais e faciais.

Na área de cidadania, os moradores terão acesso a orientações sobre o Cadastro Único (CadÚnico), emissão e parcelamento de IPTU, agendamento para isenção de documentos por meio da Fundação Leão XIII e informações da Patrulha Maria da Penha. A programação também contará com atendimento da ouvidoria da Secretaria Municipal de Saúde.

Quem precisar resolver questões relacionadas aos serviços de água, esgoto e energia elétrica também encontrará atendimento no local. A Prolagos e a Enel disponibilizarão serviços comerciais, como emissão de segunda via de contas, troca de titularidade, parcelamentos, solicitações de serviços e orientações. Já a Auto Viação Salineira participará com informações e esclarecimentos aos passageiros.

Além dos atendimentos gratuitos, o Prospera abrirá espaço para expositores e microempreendedores locais, que poderão comercializar alimentos e outros produtos durante o evento. A participação desses profissionais busca incentivar pequenos negócios e movimentar a economia local, ampliando as oportunidades para quem vive e empreende na região.

As famílias também poderão aproveitar apresentações culturais, recreação infantil e demonstração de confeitaria com degustação. Na área de educação e sustentabilidade, a programação incluirá orientações sobre cursos oferecidos pela Firjan e pela Universidade Veiga de Almeida, atividades educativas do Projeto Albatroz, Jogo do Saneamento, doação de mudas e experiências interativas. Os visitantes poderão conhecer ainda o Laboratório Móvel da Prolagos, que apresenta aspectos do controle da qualidade da água, e a Van Experience, unidade educativa da Enel.

Para organizar o fluxo de atendimento, os serviços que necessitarem de controle de vagas terão distribuição de senhas conforme a capacidade de cada atividade. A participação no evento é gratuita e não exige inscrição prévia.

“O Prospera é uma ação construída por muitas mãos, com a participação dos nossos voluntários, do poder público e de instituições parceiras. É uma oportunidade de aproximar serviços importantes da população, promover acolhimento e contribuir para a qualidade de vida das famílias. Para a Prolagos, essa mobilização também representa o compromisso de estar presente nas comunidades e contribuir para o desenvolvimento dos territórios onde atua”, destaca Aline Araújo, coordenadora de Responsabilidade Social da Prolagos.

A edição deste ano conta com o apoio da Prefeitura de São Pedro da Aldeia e de diferentes instituições que contribuirão com atendimentos e atividades durante a programação.

Mobilização nacional - Realizado pelo Instituto Aegea em parceria com as concessionárias do Grupo Aegea, o Prospera integra o Programa de Voluntariado da companhia e mobiliza colaboradores e parceiros locais para ampliar o acesso das comunidades a serviços de saúde, educação, cidadania e geração de renda. Neste ano, o evento será realizado simultaneamente em 12 municípios brasileiros, sendo São Pedro da Aldeia a única cidade do estado do Rio de Janeiro contemplada nesta edição.

Na área de atuação da Prolagos, a edição de 2025 aconteceu no bairro Jardim Esperança, em Cabo Frio, e recebeu 1.394 pessoas, com 1.177 atendimentos realizados. A mobilização reuniu voluntários e instituições parceiras para oferecer serviços e atividades gratuitas à comunidade.

Criado em 2013, o Instituto Aegea é responsável pela gestão do Investimento Social Privado do Grupo Aegea e desenvolve iniciativas voltadas ao desenvolvimento humano e territorial, com atuação nas áreas de educação, saúde e geração de renda.

articles.title: ‘Achei que era de mentira’: mulher é esfaqueada em festa de Halloween na Grande SP | G1
articles.standfirst: Vítima afirma que ataque ocorreu após outra mulher acusá-la de furar fila em bar de Itapecerica da Serra. Imagens de segurança mostram aproximação, breve troca de palavras e golpe. Mulher foi internada na UTI.
articles.summary: Vítima afirma que ataque ocorreu após outra mulher acusá-la de furar fila em bar de Itapecerica da Serra. Imagens de segurança mostram aproximação, breve troca de palavras e golpe. Mulher foi internada na UTI.
articles.body:
Uma mulher foi atingida por uma faca no pescoço após um desentendimento na fila do banheiro de um bar durante uma festa de Halloween, em Itapecerica da Serra , na Grande São Paulo. O caso aconteceu na madrugada de domingo (1º).

Segundo o boletim de ocorrência, a vítima estava com amigos no Bar Cristal Rock quando foi ao banheiro e passou a aguardar na fila. Nesse momento, começou um desentendimento com outra mulher, que teria afirmado que ela havia furado a fila.

De acordo com o registro, a discussão evoluiu para uma agressão e a outra mulher retirou uma faca da bolsa e atingiu a vítima na região do pescoço. A vítima foi ao Pronto-Socorro Central, onde recebeu atendimento.

Em um vídeo, a vítima afirmou que foi atingida no pescoço e disse que não houve briga antes do golpe. Segundo ela, houve apenas uma breve troca de palavras depois que a mulher a acusou de furar a fila e tocou em seu braço. (Assista ao vídeo abaixo)

“Ela me empurrou e falou: ‘Você pulou sim’. Eu falei que não.”

Ainda segundo a vítima, a mulher disse que iria esfaqueá-la. Por se tratar de uma festa de Halloween, ela afirmou que inicialmente não levou a ameaça a sério.

“Como era Halloween, eu não levei em consideração. [...] Eu demorei uns 10 segundos para entender porque era Halloween. Eu achei que era uma faca de mentira. Eu só me dei conta quando o sangue começou a espirrar.”

Imagens da câmera de segurança do estabelecimento mostram uma mulher se aproximando e encostando no braço da vítima. (Assista no início da matéria. ATENÇÃO: IMAGENS FORTES)

Após uma rápida troca de palavras, ela retira um objeto e faz um movimento rápido contra a região do pescoço da vítima.

Em vídeo, a vítima afirmou que teve dificuldades para engolir depois do ferimento e que permanecia internada na Unidade de Terapia Intensiva (UTI).

Segundo o relato dela, exames indicaram uma lesão em um ramo da carótida e havia possibilidade de cirurgia devido a um sangramento interno.

🔍As artérias carótidas são os principais vasos sanguíneos do pescoço e têm a função de levar sangue rico em oxigênio e nutrientes do coração para o cérebro, além de abastecer estruturas da face e do pescoço.

“Eu estou conseguindo falar, mas estou com uma dificuldade de deglutir, para comer. [...] Se eu estou viva aqui hoje, é Deus mesmo.”

Roupa de vítima ficou ensanguentada após ataque com faca. — Foto: Reprodução

Ela também afirmou que não houve uma discussão prolongada nem tempo para que pudesse se afastar antes do golpe.

“Não houve uma discussão, não houve uma ameaça para eu me afastar, nada. [...] Ela simplesmente falou e fez.”

De acordo com o boletim de ocorrência, uma faca encontrada na bolsa da mulher apontada como responsável pelo ferimento foi recolhida para perícia. Também foi solicitado exame de corpo de delito para a vítima.

Segundo o documento, duas testemunhas, a vítima e a agressora foram ouvidas.

Durante o registro do caso, a mulher apontada como responsável pelo golpe disse que não estava se sentindo bem e que fazia uso de medicamentos controlados. O Samu foi acionado para atendê-la e ela foi posteriormente encaminhada a uma unidade de saúde.

Vídeo mostra momento do esfaqueamento em bar de Itapecerica da Serra, na Grande SP. — Foto: Reprodução

Ainda de acordo com o boletim, uma equipe foi ao estabelecimento para tentar obter mais informações e imagens das câmeras de segurança, mas encontrou o local fechado.

O caso foi inicialmente registrado como lesão corporal leve e porte de arma branca e encaminhado ao Juizado Especial Criminal. A vítima também foi orientada sobre o prazo para manifestar formalmente interesse no prosseguimento do caso.

Em vídeo, a vítima classificou o episódio como um ataque e disse não compreender o motivo da agressão.

“Pelo menos eu estou viva. Isso aqui foi um ataque pessoal, eu não posso deixar isso impune.”

Ela também afirmou que identificou a mulher que aparece nas imagens e disse que pretende buscar a responsabilização pelo ocorrido.

articles.title: Trump says Russia-Ukraine deal is near after meeting Putin’s envoy
articles.summary: Though the US president said deal was ‘very close’, he gave no specifics and did not meet visiting Ukrainian delegation.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has said that a deal between Russia and Ukraine may be imminent, following a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin’s special envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, at the White House.

“I think we’re going to be very close to settling Russia-Ukraine,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on Thursday, while declining to disclose details of his conversation with Dmitriev.

“There’s going to be an agreement. It’s going to be a big agreement, and it’s going to involve more than Ukraine,” Trump said, adding that the effort could include “all of Europe”.

Trump has frequently predicted that an agreement to end Europe’s deadliest conflict since World War II was close. Negotiations have, however, picked up in recent weeks.

Trump said he did not meet the Ukrainian delegation on Thursday.

The meeting between the US president and Dmitriev came after a diplomatic gathering hosted by First Lady Melania Trump, which brought Russian and Ukrainian representatives together to mark and build on the localised six-day truce she helped broker in the southern Ukrainian city of Oleshky in October. The US president did not attend the event.

The temporary ceasefire ran from October 27 to November 1 and allowed for the evacuation of nearly 800 civilians from the besieged, Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in Ukraine’s Kherson region, as well as the delivery of critical food and medical supplies.

Senior officials from both countries attended on Thursday, including Dmitriev; Yana Lantratova, Russia’s human rights commissioner; David Arakhamia, leader of the Servant of the People party in Ukraine’s parliament; and Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine’s parliamentary human rights commissioner.

Melania Trump also spoke at the event, which the White House described as “the first time in American history that a First Lady has personally brought representatives of two nations at war to the White House for diplomacy”.

“Together, we can create something more enduring than a temporary ceasefire,” she said, urging both sides to see the humanitarian truce in Oleshky “as a spark in a world of darkness”.

The first lady presented Putin’s and Zelenskyy’s representatives with large white envelopes and asked them to deliver her personal letters to each leader. Dmitriev presented her with a painting by an 11-year-old girl, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy sent her the Order of Princess Olga, a Ukrainian award recognising her role in the ceasefire.

articles.title: Right to Buy split my estate. Now its days could be numbered
articles.summary: Labour is weakening Margaret Thatcher's landmark housing policy. Will it really fix Britain's social housing woes?
articles.body:
Growing up in a council flat in the 1980s and 1990s, my mum would often point out homes that tenants had bought from the council. You could usually tell just from looking. A plain wooden door had been replaced with something fancier. New windows had appeared. Sometimes there was a porch or pillars outside the front door.

Those houses were bought under the Right to Buy scheme - arguably the most consequential housing policy of my lifetime. It was introduced in 1980, three years before I was born, when Margaret Thatcher's government gave council tenants in England the legal right to purchase their homes at a discounted price.

Supporters welcomed the chance for working-class families to own their own home and build wealth. Critics argue it hollowed out the country's stock of social housing and contributed to today's housing crisis.

Some of my neighbours "made a killing" from the policy, in the words of my mum. One bought an almost identical flat to ours in 1989 for £21,200, after receiving a discount of £18,800. Eight years later it sold for £54,500. Five years after that it changed hands again for £143,000. (Notably, the person who made the most money from that flat wasn't the original council tenant - it was the people who bought it afterwards.)

But Andy Burnham doesn't like the policy. The Right to Buy scheme has seen various changes since its introduction in the 1980s, and Labour has weakened it significantly since coming to power in 2024. Then, in September, the prime minister told Labour's conference: "We will reform Right to Buy. Not taking the right away from anyone in an existing home, but removing it from new homes." This would help to keep council houses in public ownership "for generations to come", Burnham told delegates.

He has previously compared trying to solve the housing crisis while continuing to sell social homes to "trying to fill a bath with the plug out".

More than 40 years after its introduction, Right to Buy remains a debate about political values as much as housing policy, balancing the home ownership ideal against the desire to preserve social housing for future generations.

Since 1980, more than two million homes have been sold through the scheme in England.

In fact, about 40% of England's council housing stock has been sold through Right to Buy. Most of those sales took place in the early years, says Prof Rebecca Tunstall, a housing academic at the University of York and London School of Economics. At the time, Labour was vehemently opposed to Thatcher's plans. Yet many of its own voters went on to benefit from them.

Labour now argues that not enough of those two million homes were replaced. Sir Keir Starmer's government restricted the scheme, including by heavily reducing the maximum discount that councils were allowed to give tenants.

And now Burnham is removing the right to buy entirely from any new-build social home. The measures are included in a bill currently making its way through Parliament. The government says that before Labour's various restrictions on the scheme, England was projected to see a net loss of 26,000 council homes over the next decade. Now there will be a net gain of 18,000 homes over the same period, it calculates.

This opens up a political divide: some opposition parties, like the Conservatives and Reform UK, say they would keep or even extend the scheme.

For those who became homeowners, Right to Buy turned a dream into reality.

Barbara Stevens, now 80, bought her two-bedroom council flat in Kentish Town, north London, through Right to Buy for around £35,000. Now mortgage-free, she estimates it could be worth between £600,000 and £700,000.

"I've always wanted to own my own property," she says.

Her friend Trevor Abrahmsohn believes her story demonstrates the success of the scheme. "If you want to condemn the poor to poverty, make them lifetime renters," he says.

Those arguments were central to Thatcher's vision of a "property-owning democracy".

Few people are more closely associated with Right to Buy than Lord Heseltine, who was the cabinet minister responsible for housing when it was introduced. When he and Thatcher launched the scheme in 1980, council tenants were offered substantial discounts to purchase their homes.

A relative of mine whose parents bought their council home in Croydon told me it was the only time "anyone would ever give you a hundred grand for free".

Even Housing Secretary Angela Rayner - part of the government that's restricting Right to Buy - bought and later sold her own council home for a profit.

In 1980, Lord Heseltine described the scheme as the biggest transfer of capital wealth from the state to ordinary people. "It certainly was," he says now, almost half a century on.

I ask him if, looking back, he would have designed the policy differently. "No," he answers.

He thinks Right to Buy gave its beneficiaries an important asset. "People who bought their own homes made a great deal of capital gain," he says.

But to its detractors, Right to Buy is responsible for many of Britain's housing woes.

Prof Tunstall says the policy is partly responsible for making social housing scarcer, which meant more people competed for homes in the private rented sector, pushing up rents.

Lord Heseltine says it was originally assumed that councils would use sale proceeds to support new housing. He acknowledges that did not happen after he left government.

That failure to replace sold homes sits at the heart of the modern criticism of Right to Buy.

For Molly Harris from the New Economics Foundation, it is "private landlords [who] are the real winners".

Her think tank's research found that 41% of homes sold through Right to Buy are now privately rented out. "Homes that were built with public money, and with the aim of providing an affordable and secure path to home ownership, have since been turned into assets," Harris says.

She says the shortage of social housing means more people need help with housing costs in the private rented sector, where rents are higher. So taxpayers are effectively paying twice: once to give a discount on the initial home; and then again, via housing benefit, when that home is rented out to someone who can't afford the payments. A former council home rented privately could now be valued at double, triple or quadruple what it cost when it was under local authority control.

I put that criticism to Lord Heseltine, asking him whether the scheme has failed because some ex-council homes are now effectively being rented back to the state, at higher costs.

He dismisses it as "rubbish", adding: "The scheme was wildly successful in spreading ownership across the country."

According to Harris's research, the government spent more than £58bn between 2021 and 2025 "subsidising private landlords" through the benefit system.

Newham Council says almost half of the 9,000 council homes sold under Right to Buy in Newham were later "flipped" into private rentals. The borough now has the biggest council house waiting list in the country. Last year, The Big Issue reported that Newham Council made a loss of more than £20m of taxpayers' money buying back homes it had sold just a few years earlier. The council said it was a quick way to provide new housing, and was a cheaper option than some alternatives.

And some council tenants say they are not interested in buying their homes. Ruth Crabb has lived in her flat in Havering since 1997. "I wouldn't buy my flat because I didn't want it to go out of circulation, as social housing is for those who come after me," she says. But, she adds: "I don't judge anyone who bought their property with Right to Buy."

Supporters of Right to Buy also argue that you can't appreciate the true value of the scheme by looking at numbers on a spreadsheet.

The benefits of the policy extended for generations, they say, helping the children and grandchildren of those who bought homes.

Research co-authored by Matteo Sandi, an economics professor at the University of Milan, looked at children growing up in areas where Right to Buy uptake was highest. He found better educational and economic outcomes, including higher GCSE attainment, greater chances of attending university, and increased earnings in adulthood.

"What we find is that there is, in fact, a lasting benefit from growing up in an owned property," he says.

He believes it's because ownership encouraged families to invest more heavily in their homes and neighbourhoods.

One of my relatives backs this up. He tells me his parents were able to move elsewhere in the country, enjoy a better standard of living and finally afford things that had previously been out of reach. He believes Right to Buy transformed their lives.

But Prof Tunstall argues home ownership is not the only route to a stable family life. "The critical things for safety and for children's development and for happy families are security and affordability," she says - and children can also get that from social renting, she thinks.

When I was a child and my mum rented from the council, she knew what she would be charged every month. She knew we wouldn't suddenly be forced to move. My siblings and I knew we wouldn't have to change schools. At that point, in the 1980s, one third of houses in England were council-owned. When my mum became pregnant with me, it was safe to assume that a home would soon become available - and within about a year, one did. She moved out of my nan's and into her new council flat.

The children I now meet through my work often do not have that certainty. Today, the average wait for a family-sized home in London is 27 years. Some children are moved repeatedly between hotels and hostels. Councils across England now spend £8m every day housing families in temporary accommodation.

Sandi is careful not to present his findings as an unconditional endorsement of Right to Buy.

"My take is the Right to Buy scheme was a good policy with a big limitation," he says. "More social housing should have been built."

But curbing Right to Buy could take a long time to bear fruit, says Prof Tunstall. Scotland abolished its Right to Buy programme in 2016 and Wales followed in 2019 - but Prof Tunstall says it "hasn't made a huge difference" yet in those nations, because the changes are too recent. (Northern Ireland continues to operate a scheme similar to Right to Buy.)

And deeper challenges will remain; Right to Buy is not the only culprit of Britain's social housing shortage, she says. Supply has also been reduced by council estate-clearance programmes, she says, which saw thousands of homes demolished from the 1990s. Like Lord Heseltine, she also blames decades of under-building: had governments continued to build at their 1980s rates, she argues, the sale of council homes might not have resulted in an overall loss of social housing.

The housing landscape has also changed dramatically since 1980. Many councils transferred responsibility over council housing to housing associations, meaning they have lost the skills and expertise to build their own stock.

More than 25 years later, I return to the street where I grew up. It looks much the same, although a few new front doors suggest more homes have been sold. My mum never took advantage of Right to Buy; she continues to rent a council flat on a small estate in south London.

I ask her if she regrets that. She says she simply wouldn't have been able to afford it.

Young adults are taking prescription drugs instead of alcohol - and it's dividing experts

Publicly owned rail is popular. But is it making the trains run on time?

I tell her that the flat she could have bought for around £20,000 would now be worth somewhere between £350,000 and £400,000.

No-one in the 1980s could have known what would happen to house prices or the cost of living.

But whatever people think about Right to Buy, there is broad agreement on one point: the problem was not necessarily selling the homes. It was failing to replace them.

Additional reporting: Jade Thompson, Larissa Tairo.

articles.title: Hawaii patients may soon get prescriptions for fresh food from doctors
articles.summary: A special Medicaid program starting as soon as January aims to address chronic diet-related health issues in low-income communities.
articles.body: More than 100,000 Hawaii residents who qualify for Medicaid may soon find their doctors prescribing them fresh food as medicine. The script could be for fresh fruit and vegetables, even ahi, beef, chicken and eggs. The federally funded initiative will start as soon as January as part of a special state Medicaid program aimed at addressing chronic diet-related health issues in low-income communities. The Food Is Medicine program could help many in Hawaii, where 1 in 3 households have limited access to safe, affordable and nutritious food. It could also boost the local agricultural sector, as state advocacy and health groups have tailored the program to promote the use of local produce, which could inject millions of dollars into the economy and create almost 1,000 new jobs. “It’s really a no-brainer,” said Alicia Higa, chief health equity officer at Waiʻanae Coast Comprehensive Health Center. “If there’s an opportunity to give food as medicine to our people, we should absolutely be using that money to support the local farmers. We’ll have an increased food supply and we’ll be much better off. ... Not to mention it’s the pono thing to do.” Conventional medicine has long turned a blind eye to the importance of nutrition, but its influence on health has been gaining greater attention with the uptick in obesity and diet-related illness globally. In Hawai‘i, where food insecurity and diet-related diseases are rife, advocates hope the move will help ensure lower-income communities have sufficient food and that the food is nutritious and patients are well-versed in healthy eating. Hawaii has long held goals to address its lack of a local food supply and winnowing population of farmers, but few programs have been able to meaningfully increase the islands’ food security as it continues to be plagued by natural disasters. Now Hawaii will join at least a dozen states in implementing the nutrition scheme, enabled by the Social Security Act’s 11-15 waiver program, which allows for experimental and innovative health programs under Medicaid. The state’s program will be rolled out in three phases, starting in January with nutritional education programs and prescription food boxes for eligible patients. The program has been years in the making. Healthcare providers and advocates recommend at least 15% of all produce and protein comes from local sources, setting it apart from other states. It’s not binding, but it’s an aspiration, said Jordan Smith of Hawaii Good Food Alliance, which is one of the program’s lead agencies in the initiative. And it’s still a work in progress. “It’s a lot of work to bring together a broken healthcare system and a broken food system, and asking them to work together,” said Smith, the alliance’s Food Is Medicine program manager. Sourcing food from the continent is certainly an easier option, but healthcare providers are resolved to stay as local as possible. Otherwise, the food is mostly “coming across the ocean on a boat, it’s not fresh, it’s not necessarily culturally relevant,” Smith said. “That’s why we’re exceptionally excited about the 11-15 waiver.” Better diets, better health Big Island residents Moses and Suzette Paio have struggled with health issues associated with diet for years, making little progress in the past. What they could afford to eat plays a major role in their diet. They’re not alone, living on an island where 43% of residents report food insecurity. One-third of the state’s households report insufficient access to adequate, nutritious, affordable food, according to Hawaiʻi Food Bank’s 2025 State of Food Security Report. And about half of Native Hawaiians and Pacific Islanders are food insecure, suffering the diet-related health ramifications. Puna, where the Paios live, is classified as a food desert: a location with limited or no access to affordable, fresh, healthy and nutritious food. “It’s not that I don’t want to buy it,” Suzette Paio said, “it’s just that I can’t.” The Paios took part in a pilot program that rolled out under the Medicaid waiver this year. It included access to five months of weekly produce and protein boxes, delivered by the Food Basket, Hawaii island’s food bank. The boxes included locally caught and harvested proteins, greens and fruits. Suzette Paio’s average blood sugar has halved, something she has struggled to get under control for more than a decade. Moses Paio lost over 70 pounds. Local bananas and papayas, “they’re my candy,” said Suzette Paio, having replaced cheaper sugary treats she used to enjoy. The Paios have also started gardening, preserving food and getting more active, taking lessons from other education programs. “We just thank God for the opportunity that we had,” Suzette Paio said, “because you know our health issues have been going on for a while.” Advocates are encouraged by the data they have been collecting during pilot studies, which have run for at least the past year, though there is much more research to do. The University of Hawaii, for one, is conducting a five-year study on the program’s influence on hypertension at various healthcare centers in the islands. UH assistant professor of nutrition Monica Esquivel, who is leading the study, says much more data will come as the program develops, but its premise is proof of a growing recognition of diet’s influence on health. In West Oʻahu, also considered a food desert, nutritionally focused healthcare programs have been operating since 2017, separate from the Medicaid initiative. The positive results kept them going, said Higa, who is also ʻElepaio Social Service’s CEO. “We built it because we didn’t have it,” she said. “I think that’s traditionally what Waiʻanae does because we’re so far from everything.” During the Covid-19 pandemic, Waiʻanae Comprehensive Health Center tracked almost 500 Medicaid patients over 18 months, Higa said, when they received a $60 monthly produce prescription. Higa’s team tracked how much of the money was used, how the recipients’ health changed and how much it cost insurance. It resulted in about $118 in healthcare savings per patient, per month, she said. Now, with the Med-QUEST program, the initiative has far greater security, Higa said. Thousands could benefit Advocates believe the produce prescription will function like Hawai‘i’s Da Bux program, which doubles the spending power of beneficiaries of the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program — formerly known as food stamps — when purchasing locally produced food. There were almost 250,000 Da Bux transactions last year, accounting for more than $5.5 million in local produce, making it a triple win by benefiting the economy, the hungry and local farmers. Food Is Medicine could do the same, advocates say, given approximately 121,000 residents could be eligible for the program. The initiatives could unlock $12.3 million in additional annual revenue for Hawaii farmers, according to a national Rockefeller Foundation analysis, the lion’s share benefiting small and midize farms. It could also boost the state’s GDP by $125.5 million. The results for farmers have already been seen on Oahu, with Waiʻanae Farmers Market vendors scaling up production in response to demand driven by food-based health programs run by Waiʻanae Comprehensive. The same has happened on the Big Island, with egg producers scaling up to meet demand, according to Food Basket CEO Kristen Frost Albrecht. Micah Richards of Mauka Meats, a local meat provider, says his business and the ranchers he works with have benefited immensely. And he believes the program holds great promise for the entire agriculture sector. Some hurdles exist, Richards said, including helping farmers and ranchers get food safety certifications so they can take part. The greatest payoff from the program, he said, has been “having auntie come up to you at the market, tell you they feel better, they’re making progress with their doctor, but all they feel they changed was going to the farmers market and having access to the funds for local meat and produce.” Produce prescriptions The Medicaid program’s official rollout in January will start with prescriptions and nutritional education, but will mostly rely on organizations being able to deliver the service to eligible residents. The second phase will include helping eligible Medicaid users stock their pantries and acquire cooking supplies, as well as phasing in medically tailored meals. The meals, on a national level, could help reduce the need for 2.6 million hospitalizations annually, a net cost savings of $23.7 billion, according to Tufts University. The program is being coordinated by Med-QUEST, part of the state Department of Human Services, and the Hawaiʻi Good Food Alliance. But the programs’ full rollout will depend on individual health centers and food distributors, Med-QUEST Administrator Meredith Nichols said in an email, adding that the state is providing grants to help increase organizations’ ability to deliver the programs statewide. The prescriptions will give eligible recipients $50 per week to buy fresh protein and produce on Oʻahu, while other islands’ residents will receive $55 weekly. The food could come in the form of food boxes, like the Paios get, or in vouchers to be used at farmers markets, like Waiʻanae Coast Comprehensive Health Center’s patients do. Advocates anticipate the program will be popular. On the Big Island, Moses Paio expounds the program’s virtues openly, giving tips to friends, family and members of his church. It’s changed his life, he said, now that he’s lost weight and can be more active. “My yard pushes me. I see the grass growing,” Moses Paio said. “There are times out there, I’m cutting grass, and I’m just crying. You know, I’m just thanking God that I can even just stand there.”

articles.title: Affordability drove Baltimore voters to approve measure giving 'direct cash' to new mothers
articles.summary: Baltimore voters approved the "Baltimore Baby Fund" by a 70-30 margin, creating a permanent municipal budget line for direct cash to new parents.
articles.body: Baltimore voters approved a ballot measure Tuesday to establish a taxpayer-funded program providing cash assistance to new and expectant parents as families across the country grapple with affordability concerns. The measure, listed on the November ballot as Question I, amends the Baltimore City Charter to create a dedicated, permanent line item in the municipal budget for the Baltimore Baby Fund. It passed by roughly a 70-30 margin after organizers submitted more than the 10,000 valid signatures required to qualify for the vote. Under the approved charter amendment, the city must allocate 3 cents per $100 of assessed taxable property value directly into the dedicated fund, which is expected to generate approximately $17 million in its first year. FORMER CALIFORNIA MAYOR PUSHES GUARANTEED INCOME AS FIX FOR AFFORDABILITY CRISIS According to the mayor's office, all Baltimore City newborns enrolled in the program will be eligible for a one-time cash payment. Eligible expectant and new parents may receive additional financial assistance, such as a one-time cash payment during pregnancy or monthly cash assistance and other forms of support. The Baltimore City Council will retain authority over specific disbursement rules and eligibility criteria through future enabling legislation. The initiative was championed by grassroots organizers with the Maryland Child Alliance alongside Baltimore Mayor Brandon Scott, who serves as a national co-chair of Mayors for Guaranteed Income. "We aren’t surprised that Baltimore voters saw the value in a baby fund to offer new parents direct cash," Shafeka Hashash, director of cash initiatives at the Economic Security Project (ESP), told Fox News Digital. The ESP, an organization that has backed the creation of dozens of guaranteed income programs nationwide, pointed to mounting cost-of-living pressures facing American families as a primary catalyst for direct cash initiatives. "Right now, as the cost of the basics like groceries, gas, healthcare and childcare continues to rise, paychecks haven’t kept up, and families can’t make ends meet," Hashash said. "Then, for new parents, the affordability crisis is compounded by an increase in new costs; this is why poverty rises 45% from the last month of pregnancy to the first month after birth." PRO-LIFE VS SOCIALISM: GOP LAWMAKERS DIVIDED OVER CONTROVERSIAL GUARANTEED INCOME PROGRAMS Hashash noted that direct financial support provides immediate relief during a critical transition window for families. "In that exact critical moment, direct cash can cover everyday essentials like diapers or a new crib, or it can offer relief on the bigger financial strains, like the maternity ward bills or daycare payment," Hashash added. "Voters understood this policy implicitly because it’s simple, and we know it will be efficient and effective. We are excited to see how Baltimore benefits with this new resource for families." According to Baltimore public radio station WYPR, Emily Yu, campaign manager for the effort, praised the grassroots momentum behind the measure. "We are public servants and community members that wanted to make this happen, and it's pretty unbelievable that we made it happen," Yu reportedly said. "But it just speaks to the people power in Baltimore City. Clearly, there's an appetite for it, so I would encourage other groups to do the same." NEWSOM'S 'GOLDEN STATE START' PROMISES 400 FREE DIAPERS PER BABY AS CALIFORNIA GRAPPLES WITH BUDGET WOES Advocates with national guaranteed income coalitions also celebrated the ballot outcome. "People are excited about the idea of cash for new and expecting families because it works. We heard from Americans loud and clear on Tuesday that families across the political spectrum are concerned about two things: affordability and healthcare," Tegan Lecheler, national program director of the Mother & Infant Cash Coalition, told Fox News Digital. Founded in 2023, the Mother & Infant Cash Coalition grew out of a broader movement toward direct financial support for young families. Lecheler, who previously managed operations with The Bridge Project, an unrestricted cash transfer initiative launched in 2021 operating across multiple states, noted that momentum for direct cash assistance built rapidly during the COVID-19 pandemic. Lecheler argued that providing cash directly to families demonstrates that local governments are responsive to constituents' needs. "Programs giving cash to new families address both, and this ballot measure's passage is a clear example of government delivering results and being responsive to the concerns of constituents. The affordability crisis isn't something that gets left at home. It comes with voters to the voting booth. Politicians that listen and prioritize the issues that Americans face every day will likely continue to be successful," Lecheler said. The ballot measure builds on previous direct cash programs in the city. Mayor Scott previously oversaw the Baltimore Young Families Success Fund, a pilot program that operated from August 2022 to July 2024. The program provided unconditional monthly payments of $1,000 to 200 low-income parents ages 18 to 24 earning at or below 300% of the federal poverty level using funds from the American Rescue Plan Act. articles.title: Fox News bests MS NOW, CNN as most-watched cable news network on 2026 midterm election night
articles.summary: Fox News Channel led all cable news networks on midterm election night as Democrats swept both the House and Senate in a historic blue tsunami.
articles.body: Fox News Channel was America's most-watched cable news network Tuesday night as results from the 2026 midterm elections rolled in. According to the final Nielsen election night rating data, Fox News bested both CNN and MS NOW with an average of 4.3 million total viewers during primetime. CNN came in second with 4.1 million total average viewers. MS NOW marked the network's first major election night since its rebranding by finishing third with 3.7 million total average viewers. FOX, USVETS RENEW 'MAKE CAMO YOUR CAUSE' CAMPAIGN DEDICATED TO ENDING VETERAN HOMELESSNESS Fox News also thrived in the digital landscape on election night. Fox News Digital had double-digit spikes in key metrics across the board during coverage of the midterms. Fox News also registered 3.3 million social media interactions across social media platforms, including Facebook, X, Instagram and TikTok, according to Emplifi and Comscore Social. Fox News also reached 15.4 million YouTube video views, according to Emplifi. FOX NEWS CONTINUES CABLE NEWS LEAD OVER MS NOW, CNN IN OCTOBER VIEWERSHIP "Fox News Democracy 26" was co-anchored by Bret Baier and Martha MacCallum. They were joined throughout the night by Dana Perino, Brit Hume, Harold Ford Jr., Bill Hemmer, Sandra Smith, Laura Ingraham, Jesse Watters, Sean Hannity and other Fox News personalities. President Donald Trump also called in and spoke with Baier and MacCallum with his reaction to the midterm results. Democrats had a historic night, retaking both the House and Senate in what's been widely described as a blue tsunami. While recapturing the House was expected, Democrats stunned with Senate pickups in states like South Carolina, Texas, Kansas and Iowa. It is unclear whether Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., will have enough votes in his caucus to reclaim the title of Senate majority leader after several newly elected Democrats previously said they won't back him. articles.title: 35+ gifts for teens they’ll actually use, according to the teens in our lives
articles.summary: Looking for gifts for teenage girls and boys? Discover our picks for stylish, practical and personalized presents, with recommendations from real teens.
articles.body: Shopping for teenagers can be tricky. Trends come and go, interests change seemingly overnight and what was considered cool a few months ago might already be out of style. And while teenagers are often pretty vocal about what they like (and especially what they don’t like), finding a gift they’ll actually use and appreciate long term can still feel like a guessing game. Luckily, I have a few teenagers in my corner. As the oldest of three siblings, including a 16-year-old sister, and as an occasional tutor for high schoolers, I’ve had a front-row seat to the changing trends of today’s teens. I am very good at giving gifts, according to everyone I know. Every year, I arrange dozens of gifts for my large family across many age groups and they all ask me, “how do you do it?” Shopping and testing products for a living helps, but I truly take pride in giving people gifts that make them feel special, and won’t just get added to piles of clutter somewhere. Whether you’re shopping for a fashion-obsessed 13-year-old, a high school athlete or a soon-to-be college student, these are some of the best gifts for teens to consider this year. The best gifts for teens in 2026 With trends coming and going faster than ever, teens are constantly being told what they should want next. As a big sister, I want my siblings to discover their own taste and understand that the best things aren’t always the trendiest. These gifts strike that balance, with picks that feel exciting now but are useful and special enough to enjoy long after the hype fades. Best clothing gifts for teens My 16-year-old sister owns this jacket in three colors and hopes to collect more like they’re Infinity Stones. It’s one of her favorite pieces to wear to school, sports practice and just about everywhere else. Made from Lululemon’s soft, stretchy, sweat-wicking fabric, the Define Jacket has a fitted silhouette, zippered pockets and thumbholes with fold-over cuffs to help keep hands warm. For teens who prefer something roomier, my sister also recommends the brand’s Scuba Evolve Hoodie, which is great for lounging, running errands or layering over workout clothes. Growing up, my mother would make us wear the thickest long johns underneath our school uniforms during the winter. Between the sweating, chafing and bulkiness, I dreaded putting them on. Thankfully, thermal wear has come a long way. I own this cashmere-blend top from Etam in black and blue, and it’s become a cold-weather essential for me. It’s lightweight enough to wear underneath sweaters and jackets without adding bulk, but stylish enough to wear on its own. Think of it as an elevated alternative to traditional thermals. I hate layering leggings or thermals underneath my jeans when it’s cold outside, which is why I’ve become such a fan of DUER’s fleece-lined denim. The brand’s Tech Fleece fabric combines the look of denim with the comfort and warmth of an insulating layer, helping keep me cozy without needing to double up on pants. I own a pair and have found them particularly useful during colder months. NBC Selected reporter Zoe Malin recommends Duer’s high-rise straight-leg jeans if the teen you’re shopping for prefers a classic denim silhouette. Ugg’s Classic Ultra Mini boots are a great gift for teens who love cozy footwear. Their low-cut silhouette makes them easy to slip on and style with leggings, jeans or sweatpants, while the sheepskin lining adds warmth during colder months. They’re especially useful for casual outings, long travel days, quick errands and lounging between activities. For the teen who’s always keeping up with sneaker trends, Adidas’ Samba OG is a versatile option. Originally designed as an indoor soccer shoe, the low-profile sneaker has become a casual wardrobe staple that pairs easily with jeans, skirts and wide-leg trousers. If the recipient already owns a pair, consider another Adidas style like the Barreda Lo, Japan or Gazelle Indoor shoes. Every teen has a pair of Crocs and their special collection of Jibbitzs. My sister and I have multiples and we welcome new ones every year with gratitude. They’re just so practical. Best winter jacket gifts for teens Aritzia’s Super Puff is a splurge, but its serious warmth and stylish, oversized look make it a teen gift worth considering. Toronto native and associate reporter Ashley Morris says, “I’ve never had a coat this warm before,” noting she can brave freezing temperatures with just a T-shirt underneath. With multiple lengths, colors and finishes, plus deep pockets for their phone, keys and lip gloss, it’s as practical as it is cool-looking. The North Face is a reliable option for winter outerwear, and I own a jacket from the brand. The 1996 Retro Nuptse is one of its most recognizable styles, featuring a boxy silhouette, oversized quilted sections and 700-fill recycled down insulation for warmth. It also has a water-repellent finish and a stowable hood. For teens who want a jacket they can wear to school, on weekend outings and during cold-weather activities, it’s a versatile option worth considering for any teen in your life. My 16-year-old sister bought this jacket from Hollister for herself, and it’s become one of her favorite winter purchases. I can see why: The reversible design gives her two different looks in one, with a classic quilted puffer on one side and cozy faux fur on the other. It also has a hood with removable faux fur trim, lined pockets and thumbholes at the cuffs. It’s an especially good gift for fashion-conscious teens who enjoy switching up their style without having to own multiple winter coats. Best bags and accessories gifts for teens When I asked my 16-year-old sister what teenagers actually wanted for Christmas, this backpack was the first thing she mentioned. As a student athlete herself, it was at the very top of her wish list. It has a spacious main compartment that can accommodate a full-size basketball, plus a separate bottom compartment for shoes or sweaty clothes. It’s a practical, gender-neutral option for teens balancing school, sports and extracurricular activities, especially those who need something roomy enough to carry their gear throughout the day. In my opinion, Coach has had one of the best brand revivals in recent years, and my sister agrees. She sends links to handbags, shoes and accessories from the brand to our family group chat practically every week. For teens interested in starting a handbag collection, I recommend the Coach Plaza Bag. Its simple, streamlined design makes it easy to dress up or down, while its compact size is convenient for carrying everyday essentials. Another option I love is the Coach Brooklyn Shoulder Bag 28, which has a more relaxed silhouette and offers more space inside. For teens who prefer a structured, functional bag, the Coach Utility Tote is worth considering. articles.title: California governor commutes sentences of more than 500 people on death row
articles.summary: Gavin Newsom cites state values and flaws in the legal system as he grants largest mass clemency in US history.
articles.body:
California Governor Gavin Newsom has announced that he will commute the sentences of all 548 people on death row in the state, the largest mass clemency in United States history.

The announcement on Thursday effectively clears out California’s death row , although the state has not executed a prisoner for 20 years. Those on death row will instead serve life sentences without the possibility of parole.

“I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us,” Newsom said in an open letter.

Support for the death penalty in the US has largely declined since the 1990s, although it still holds majority backing.

A Pew Research Center poll released in August found that 66 percent of Americans supported the punishment for those convicted of murder. Roughly 73 percent, however, acknowledged there was a risk of executing an innocent person.

Because death penalty cases often involve long and arduous legal appeals, many of those on death row are never executed.

Twenty-three states have banned the practice outright, and others have effectively abandoned it even if the punishment remains on the books.

Still, President Donald Trump, a Republican, has championed the death penalty for serious federal crimes. In April, his administration pledged to expand the use of federal executions, including by employing firing squads.

While proponents of the death penalty have argued that the punishment has a deterrent effect, critics say decades of scholarship indicate otherwise.

They have also pointed to ethical and logistical issues, including the expense.

According to the Death Penalty Information Center (DPIC), California has spent $6bn on the death penalty since 1978 while carrying out just 13 executions in that time.

Capital punishment has also been criticised for being applied disproportionately to racial minorities and for the frequency of botched executions .

The DPIC says that, since 1973, at least 203 people wrongly convicted and sentenced to death in the US have later been exonerated.

Newsom’s decision has been praised by criminal justice groups as a step away from a practice they say is outdated, inefficient and immoral.

“Governor Newsom’s announcement marks a decisive moment in the history of the death penalty in the United States. Though other governors have granted universal clemencies, none have been at this scale,” Robin Maher, the executive director of the DPIC, said in a statement.

“By bookending his time as governor first with a moratorium and now this mass clemency, Governor Newsom has irrevocably changed California’s relationship with the death penalty.”

The DPIC noted that about two-thirds of the commutations must be reviewed by the California Supreme Court, which is required under state law to review clemency for anyone with multiple felony convictions, before they become final.

Despite its left-leaning reputation, California previously served as a laboratory for punitive criminal justice policies in the late 20th century, during the heyday of the US’s tough-on-crime politics.

The states of Washington and California, for instance, were among the first to pass “three strikes” laws in the early 1990s, punishing repeat offenders with high minimum sentences.

The state continues to have the largest death row in the country.

Newsom’s decision will reduce the number of people on death row nationally by nearly 30 percent.

The announcement also comes days after a blockbuster night for the Democratic Party in the US midterm elections , with major wins in formerly right-wing strongholds such as Texas and Kansas.

The so-called “blue wave” during the midterms has set off speculation over potential Democratic candidates for the presidency in 2028.

As governor for nearly eight years, Newsom has reached California’s term limits: His second and final term will end in January 2027.

He will be replaced by former US Secretary of Health and Human Services Xavier Becerra on January 4.

But Newsom has long been seen as a likely presidential contender , and he has increasingly dedicated time to serving as a proxy to support Democratic candidates in key races nationwide.

He has, however, taken positions on criminal justice issues that have put him at odds with criminal justice groups and the state legislature.

In 2022, Newsom vetoed a bill that would have placed limits in state prisons on the use of solitary confinement , a practice defined as torture by the United Nations after certain lengths of time.

In 2019, he also vetoed a measure that would have limited cooperation between Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and prison authorities, and a similar bill failed in the state Senate in 2022.

articles.title: 'The View' co-host confronts Abdul El-Sayed on his response to attack on Jewish Synagogue
articles.summary: "The View" co-host Sara Haines pressed Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed on his delayed apology for his "hurt people hurt people" remarks after the Temple Israel attack in Michigan.
articles.body: "The View" co-host Sara Haines pressed Michigan Senator-elect Abdul-El Sayed about his response to an attack on a Jewish synagogue in the state and his delay in apologizing for his comments. On March 12, a man drove a truck into Temple Israel in West Bloomfield Township and exchanged gunfire with security personnel before killing himself, according to authorities. El-Sayed condemned the attack but drew criticism for subsequently saying, "Hurt people hurt people," referring to the attacker's relatives who had been killed in an Israeli airstrike in Lebanon. ABDUL EL-SAYED HITS BACK AT ISRAEL QUESTIONS, SUGGESTS HIS NAME AND FAITH ARE BEHIND PRESS SCRUTINY "Your response, that ‘Hurt people hurt people’ after the Temple Israel attack in Michigan in March really stuck with a lot of people," Haines said. "And you did apologize for that. But it took you a while to. It took about five months to seemingly understand why that landed wrong with people and voters and constituents. You know, do you think that leaders have a responsibility to challenge the extremist views in their own religion, especially considering you're the first Muslim senator of the United States?" she asked. "Yeah, well, I really appreciate that question," El-Sayed said. "And I agree with you entirely that we want to live in a world where faith is something that's used to uplift all of us, rather than to justify the worst human actions that sometimes drag us down." He recalled having visited the temple after the attack and having been there for a bar mitzvah in his youth. "You know, I condemned it immediately, and I wanted to offer context, but ... you know, when people are hurting, context is secondary, and I just should have stood with their pain. And I learned from that experience. And I'm not above apologizing when I make a mistake," he said. El-Sayed continued and said he had tried to "offer context around the fact that that individual had lost a child, niece and nephew in an airstrike. And I want us to be thinking a little bit about, A, how we demonstrate our ability as leaders to stand with people's pain with no exceptions and no asterisks around them. And also be able to have an adult conversation about the ways in which actions ricochet around the world and create worse for all of us." 'THE VIEW' CO-HOSTS DEFEND EL-SAYED COMPARING HIMSELF TO JFK OVER MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD SCRUTINY "I respect that. I just think that if that had been done anywhere near what I believed, I would be so furiously enraged that they would use the words that I have led my life with to hurt people that way," Haines said. "And that was young kids. So, I just was surprised it took a minute for you to understand that part." "I hear you on that," El-Sayed said. "Better late than never," co-host Joy Behar said. Jesse Arm, a vice president at the Manhattan Institute and a pollster originally from Michigan, told Fox News Digital, "Imagine an American politician responding to Dylann Roof’s massacre of Black worshipers at Bible study by saying ‘Hurt people hurt people,’ then asking us to consider the killer’s grievances. That politician would rightly be run out of American public life." "Why should the standard be any different when the targets are Jewish children and the attacker is an Islamist?" Arm continued. "El-Sayed’s comments were grotesque, and this interview compounds the problem. He’s still presenting his mistake as a matter of timing as though the same rationalization would have been acceptable once the victims had time to grieve. The problem wasn’t when he offered it. The problem was suggesting that events overseas somehow mitigate responsibility for trying to massacre Americans at home." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Whatever someone has suffered, there is no justification for attacking a synagogue full of children. None," Arm wrote. "Americans deserve leaders who can say that without pivoting to the terrorist’s pain. Our politics is in a dangerous place when that basic moral clarity becomes negotiable depending on the identities of the attacker and the intended victims," he continued.

articles.title: Dolly Parton estate files to dismiss lawsuit against her nephew
articles.summary: The company that manages Parton’s estate had accused her nephew of threatening to destroy her brand.
articles.body: The company that manages Dolly Parton’s estate asked a court Thursday to dismiss its legal claims against the singer’s nephew, weeks after it accused him of threatening the icon’s legacy. She’s Alive LLC, which manages Parton’s estate, in September filed a lawsuit and sought a restraining order against Bryan Seaver, Parton’s nephew and owner of a company that provided the security detail for the singer. On Thursday, She’s Alive filed a motion to dismiss the civil claims against Seaver in a brief one-paragraph notice. The request was to dismiss the case without prejudice, which means it could be refiled. It was not immediately clear whether that would be pursued or if the matter was being dropped. Attorneys for She’s Alive and Seaver did not immediately respond to requests for comment Thursday evening. Parton, the beloved country music icon, died in August at 80. She had cancer. In late September, She’s Alive filed a lawsuit alleging that Seaver had, among other things, threatened to “set up a podcast dedicated to ruining Dolly’s brand partnerships.” She’s Alive had fired Seaver and his company in mid-September, it said in the suit. The estate manager sought a restraining order against Seaver. In October, the estate accused Seaver of using items to barricade his property in an attempt to avoid being served with a lawsuit. Seaver in a court filing denied accusations that he had threatened the estate, telling the court the messages were taken out of context and were about a specific business dispute. According to Seaver, the situation stemmed from a dispute between his security company and the company that operates Parton’s hotel and museum in downtown Nashville. Seaver’s company, Squadron Augmented Protection Services, provided security for the hotel and was owed approximately $251,000 for services rendered, an affidavit filed by Seaver said.
