articles.title: Indiana, Florida and Alabama carry out rare US triple execution day
articles.summary: Three inmates were executed by lethal injection in Indiana, Florida and Alabama on the same day, the second time that has happened in 2026.
articles.body: Indiana, Florida and Alabama each put a man to death Thursday, the second time this year that three inmates were executed in the U.S. the same day. The first triple execution this year took place Aug. 13, when Oklahoma, Tennessee and Alabama executed inmates within hours of each other. Before Aug. 13, the last time three executions were carried out in the U.S. on the same day was Jan. 7, 2010. On Thursday, Indiana officials put to death the first inmate of the day when it executed Jeffrey Weisheit, 50, for setting a 2010 house fire that killed his girlfriend's two children, ages 8 and 5, as the couple's relationship deteriorated. He was pronounced dead at 12:45 a.m. at the Indiana State Prison in Michigan City after receiving a lethal injection. His attorneys sought permission for additional brain scans, arguing that his history of head injuries and mental health problems warranted further examination. Republican Gov. Mike Braun denied the request. Braun also rejected appeals to commute Weisheit's death sentence to life in prison. INDIANA EXECUTES MAN CONVICTED OF KILLING 2 CHILDREN AS MORE US EXECUTIONS LOOM THURSDAY Weisheit's lawyers had also raised separate concerns about Indiana's planned use of execution drugs obtained from a pharmacy facing a disciplinary hearing before the Indiana Pharmacy Board next week. But the Indiana Department of Correction maintained it was confident in its ability to carry out the execution "humanely." After the execution, Braun said Weisheit's case had undergone repeated reviews in state and federal courts. "These reviews have never resulted in an overturned sentence," Braun said in a statement. "Today, Weisheit's sentence has been carried out as ordered by the court." The execution provided "long-awaited justice for Alyssa Lynch and her brother Caleb, two innocent children whose lives were stolen in an act of unspeakable cruelty," Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita said. In Florida, Jesse Guardado, 64, was executed after confessing and pleading guilty to fatally stabbing a 75-year-old woman who had helped him find a job and housing in 2004. Guardado killed Jackie Malone inside her home before stealing her jewelry box, $80 and other items to fund his drug addiction. Guardado was pronounced dead at 6:13 p.m. following a lethal injection at Florida State Prison near Starke. Florida's latest execution matched last year's state record total of 19 inmates put to death in a single year. Florida has ramped up executions after Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis signed a series of death warrants since 2025. The state's 19 executions last year was more than under any other Florida governor in a single year since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976. Those executions accounted for roughly 40% of the 47 carried out nationwide in 2025. FLORIDA PUTS 77-YEAR-OLD MAN TO DEATH FOR DEPUTY'S MURDER AS STATE CLOSES IN ON EXECUTION RECORD The Sunshine State has also accounted for more than half of the 35 executions carried out nationwide, which includes Thursday's executions. In July, Florida executed two prisoners on the same day, the first double execution by a single state in nearly a decade. Alabama capped off the triple execution day by putting Michael Taylor, 54, to death for the 1991 murders of an older couple who were beaten to death with a metal bar during a robbery inside their home. Authorities caught Taylor in Birmingham, about an hour away, with the victims' Cadillac. Taylor was executed by lethal injection after a judge ruled against his attorneys' objections to the method. Taylor had previously requested execution by nitrogen gas, and his attorneys sought to preserve that choice. His attorneys said he "knew the depth of the harm he caused" and "grieved it for the rest of his life." They also said he became a changed man while behind bars, saying, "Michael’s life was proof that God isn’t finished with any of us. Tonight we pray that both families find peace, and we deeply mourn the loss of Michael." Death penalty opponents had urged Republican Gov. Kay Ivey to commute Taylor's sentence to life in prison, arguing that he was too young and immature at 19 to fully understand the consequences of his actions. But the governor declined to stop the execution. Ivey issued a statement on Thursday night describing his actions as "reprehensible." "Thirty-five years ago yesterday, Ivan and Lucille Moore kindly opened their home to Michael Taylor. Mr. Taylor repaid the Moores by beating them to death with a metal bar, all to rob them for money to buy clothing and jewelry," she said. The victims' family thanked the state attorney general's office for bringing closure to the case but expressed disappointment for having to wait 35 years to see the death sentence carried out. For all these years, our family has had to live with the waiting, the delays, and the uncertainty," the statement read. "We have never forgotten our loved ones or what was taken from us." The executions come amid renewed scrutiny of lethal injection procedures following a failed execution attempt in Tennessee, where death row inmate Christa Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital and was rushed to a hospital in late September. She has since been released from the hospital and returned to prison. Thursday's executions came on the same day California Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom announced he is seeking to commute all 548 death sentences in the Golden State to life without parole, though 382 of the commutations require a recommendation from the California Supreme Court, saying he believes "state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us." Newsom, who put a moratorium on executions in the state in 2019, said he "knew we cannot execute people in our imperfect legal system and remain true to our core values, the first among them justice and human decency." articles.title: Iran’s security chief meets Putin, delivers message from Khamenei
articles.summary: Putin meets Iran’s top security official to discuss regional security and receives a letter from Mojtaba Khamenei.
articles.body:
Russia’s President Vladimir Putin has met Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei in Moscow to discuss regional security as diplomatic efforts gather pace to end the United States and Israel’s war on Iran.

During the meeting on Thursday, Rezaei also delivered a letter to Putin from Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, according to the Iranian state broadcaster Press TV.

Speaking after the meeting, Rezaei said the talks had focused on security arrangements in the region, as well as Russia’s support for ending what he called the US’s “aggression” against Iran.

“Important regional issues were discussed with Putin and significant conversations took place regarding the post-war period and regional security arrangements,” he said.

Other topics, he said, included plans to deepen energy cooperation, including building gas pipelines from Russia to Iran.

Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said Khamenei had wanted him to deliver the message to Putin as soon as possible. The trip to Moscow had been planned nearly a month earlier, he said, but was postponed due to “daily discussions about the military situation in the region”.

He did not say what the message contained.

Khamenei said in a written statement on Wednesday that there should not be “even the slightest inclination towards submission” to the US. He also called for an “ever stronger” Iran to reach a “point of absolute deterrence”.

Rezaei’s meeting with Putin came as Qatar steps up diplomatic efforts to end the war on Iran amid fears the US could renew attacks following its midterm elections.

In Tuesday’s vote, US President Donald Trump’s Republican Party lost control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate amid widespread anger over rising prices that many blame on the war on Iran.

Efforts to end the conflict have centred on the future status of the strategic Strait of Hormuz, a US blockade of Iranian ports, sanctions against Iran, and a resumption of negotiations over the country’s nuclear programme.

Rezaei said on Thursday that Tehran would not hold talks with the US on ending the war and reopening the Strait of Hormuz until Washington meets its seven demands .

“On the issue of diplomacy, we have announced seven conditions to the Americans. As long as they do not execute our seven conditions, we will neither open the Strait of Hormuz nor have negotiations,” he said.

According to Rezaei, Putin reiterated that Russia is ready to provide support to end the war. Last month, Putin told Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian that Russia was prepared to “ do everything ” it could towards that end, Russian news agencies reported.

Rezaei said the discussion at the Kremlin also focused on the construction of a gas pipeline from Russia to Iran, aimed at addressing Iran’s gas shortages and enabling Russia to sell its gas to countries neighbouring Iran.

He added that he had briefed Putin on a meeting held in Tehran in late October among Iran, Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan, and that the Russian leader had welcomed it.

“Like our Chinese friends, we believe that there should be regional arrangements and that foreign countries should not interfere in the security of the region,” he said.

The Kremlin did not immediately release its own account of the meeting, which took place in the Senate Palace, according to Russia’s TASS news agency.

Separately, Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi held phone calls with his counterparts in Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Oman, Qatar, Turkiye and Jordan.

His calls focused on regional developments and ongoing diplomatic efforts to promote peace, Iranian state media reported.

Russia and Iran, both under heavy Western sanctions, have strengthened their diplomatic and military ties in recent years.

In January 2025, they signed a comprehensive strategic partnership treaty covering trade, military cooperation, science, culture and education.

The treaty took effect that October, but unlike Russia’s pact with North Korea, it does not include a mutual defence clause.

On Saturday, Iranian army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia said Iran had bought Russian Su-35 fighter jets and expected to receive them after the war ends.

The planes were originally supposed to arrive before the fighting began, he told the Iranian news site Tabnak, and the necessary preparations and pilot training were complete.

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Delhi continued to reel under high pollution levels on Friday, with the city’s overall Air Quality Index (AQI) recorded at 389 in the ‘very
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Delhi continued to reel under high pollution levels on Friday, with the city’s overall Air Quality Index (AQI) recorded at 389 in the ‘very poor’ category at 8 am, according to the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB).Several areas in the national capital reported AQI levels in the ‘severe’ category. IIT Delhi and Rohini recorded an AQI of 474 each, followed by Punjabi Bagh at 465, RK Puram at 443, ITO at 422, Firoz Shah Road at 420 and India Gate at 403, according to CPCB data.Meanwhile, municipal authorities deployed truck-mounted water sprinklers around India Gate to carry out water sprinkling operations under Stage II of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP).Other areas also reported high pollution levels. Anand Vihar and Akshardham recorded an AQI of 359, while IGI Airport Terminal 3 registered 385. The AQI stood at 393 in Aya Nagar and 391 in Chandni Chowk.According to the India Meteorological Department (IMD), Delhi recorded a minimum morning temperature of 17.8°C, with skies remaining mainly clear. The weather department has forecast shallow fog over the next four days, followed by fog or mist during early morning hours on November 10 and 11.Residents continued to report discomfort due to the deteriorating air quality. A local resident, Sarvesh, said the pollution had made breathing difficult and was causing irritation in the eyes."It's causing a lot of problems. As you can see, it's morning, and there isn't much traffic, but because of the pollution, it's hard to breathe, and I'm feeling anxious. There's a lot of smog, making it feel like the middle of January. So, there are a lot of issues, like a burning sensation in the eyes," he said.Another local, Nemichand Sharma, said that the crisis feels like the predictable consequence of unchecked urbanisation and administrative apathy."I am seventy-one years old now. And ever since Delhi has developed, the progress and development in the name of development has brought about a huge increase in pollution. They have been given a free pass: wherever dirt is going to spread, just let it spread. Do whatever you want. And every day, instead of showing the pollution from Akshardham and solving the problem, governments are doing nothing with all their machinery except making money in the name of pollution. There is no ground-level work to end pollution," he said.Earlier on Thursday, Delhi Environment Minister Manjinder Singh Sirsa accused Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann of misleading people over paddy harvesting and stubble burning. Sirsa said stubble burning in Punjab had contributed significantly to the deteriorating air quality in the national capital.Addressing the media at the Integrated Command and Control Centre (ICCC) in Shastri Park, Sirsa claimed that 77% of the stubble had already been burnt, citing data from the Punjab government."Yesterday, Bhagwant Mann held a press conference and falsely claimed that the harvesting of paddy has not yet begun; however, according to the data provided by his own government, 77 per cent of the stubble (parali) has already been burnt," he said.(With Agency Inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: 'Long road ahead': Eisenkot beats Netanyahu 67-46 in backing but government test looms
articles.summary: Israel's Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot has secured the backing of 67 members of the Knesset to receive the mandate to form Israel's next government.
articles.body: Israel's Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot has secured the backing of 67 members of the Knesset to receive the mandate to form Israel's next government. This has also put him ahead of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.However, despite the strong endorsement, Eisenkot faces a difficult task in building a coalition. Several parties that are backing his candidature are also unwilling to join his government.Eisenkot secured the support during consultations with Israeli President Isaac Herzog on Thursday, after the Arab-led Joint List unanimously decided to recommend him for the prime ministerial mandate. He has reiterated his goal of forming a "national emergency government" to bring political stability to Israel.In a post on X, Eisenkot said the first round of discussions with the opposition parties had concluded with an absolute majority of recommendations in his favour. He, however, acknowledged that the road to forming a government remained long."First round of talks and meetings this week with the Change and Repair parties. This evening, the round of consultations at the President's Residence was completed with an absolute majority of recommenders for the purpose of receiving the mandate from the President of the State to form a government. The goal: The establishment of a national emergency government that will return our dear country to safety and sanity. The road ahead of us is still long; we are very determined. We will do it, and we will succeed," he wrote.Eisenkot's 67 endorsements comprise 48 lawmakers from the Jewish-led opposition bloc, including Yashar, Together, The Democrats and Yisrael Beiteinu. The Ra'am party contributed eight seats, while the Joint List added 11.Netanyahu, meanwhile, received recommendations from only 46 lawmakers, down from the 53 seats previously expected to back him. His traditional ally, United Torah Judaism (UTJ), refused to recommend either candidate, leaving the prime minister with a reduced tally.According to a report by Times of Israel, the Joint List's decision proved crucial in giving Eisenkot a decisive lead over Netanyahu. The party had earlier indicated that it might abstain but eventually announced its support during Thursday's consultations.Joint List chairman Yousef Jabareen defended the move, saying the party wanted to prevent Netanyahu from returning to power."We will do everything to remove the greatest threat to all of us, which is the continuation of the rule of Netanyahu and his Kahanist partners," he said in a post on X.Forming a government remains difficult for Netanyahu's rivalDespite crossing the 61-seat majority mark during the presidential consultations, Eisenkot's endorsements do not necessarily translate into support for an actual governing coalition.The Joint List has made clear that it has significant policy disagreements with parts of the Jewish opposition's platform. It has also ruled out formally joining an Eisenkot-led coalition, although it could support the government from outside.The Times of Israel reported that only 48 of the 67 lawmakers who recommended Eisenkot are currently prepared to work together without conditions. This is five fewer than the 53-seat bloc Netanyahu was expected to command before UTJ withheld its recommendation.The possibility of securing UTJ's support also presents difficulties. The ultra-Orthodox party is a key player in the dispute over exemptions from military service for Haredi men. Its demands on the issue are at odds with the positions of several parties in Eisenkot's camp.Yisrael Beiteinu leader Avigdor Liberman has also ruled out forming a government that depends on support from Arab parties, making it harder for Eisenkot to rely on the Joint List and Ra'am.The Times of Israel noted that Netanyahu and his allies could also use the prospect of an opposition government relying on Arab party support to undermine Eisenkot's political ambitions. The Likud-led campaign questioning the legitimacy of Arab political participation could intensify if such an arrangement takes shape.Eisenkot now has the political momentum, but converting the recommendations into a workable majority will be his biggest challenge. Unlike Netanyahu, who has a long record of navigating complex coalition negotiations, Eisenkot has relatively little experience in political horse-trading.Herzog to hold further consultationsAlthough Eisenkot received recommendations from more than the 61 lawmakers required for a Knesset majority, the Israeli President Herzog has not yet formally assigned him the mandate to form the government.According to ANI, the president will hold further consultations with political parties before deciding on Sunday whom to task with forming the next government.According to the Times of Israel report, Herzog had also attempted to explore the possibility of a national unity arrangement during Thursday's meetings. However, Eisenkot's camp signalled its opposition to sharing power with Netanyahu.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Two Iowa families donated adjoining properties worth 21 acres in the US, turning privately owned land into a public recreation area while giving local wildlife a protected natural space
articles.summary: In Pocahontas County, Iowa, two neighbouring parcels of land have found a new purpose through a donation that will keep them available for wildlife and
articles.body: In Pocahontas County, Iowa, two neighbouring parcels of land have found a new purpose through a donation that will keep them available for wildlife and public recreation. The properties, given by two families, cover a combined 21 acres of mixed habitat and natural space south of Pocahontas. Rather than remaining under private ownership, the land was transferred to Pocahontas County Conservation, allowing it to serve the wider community while retaining its value as a habitat for local wildlife. The donation formed part of a wider conservation effort in Iowa during 2025, when individuals, families and organisations helped protect thousands of acres across the state.How 10-acre and 11-acre donations in the US became one conservation propertyThe 21-acre contribution came from John L. Pascal, Jr. and Sally J. Pascal, who donated a 10-acre parcel to the Iowa Natural Heritage Foundation (INHF). Their property was joined by an adjoining 11 acres given by Gail Ewan, creating a larger stretch of land that could be managed for conservation and public use.Both parcels are located south of Pocahontas in Pocahontas County. Their proximity made it possible for the two donations to be brought together under a single conservation arrangement, rather than treated as separate pieces of land.Following the donations, ownership of the properties was transferred to Pocahontas County Conservation. The county body will oversee the area as a public recreation space, while the land's natural character provides an opportunity to retain habitat for wildlife.The conservation process behind the 21-acre Iowa land donationThe donations were made through the Iowa Natural Heritage Foundation, a nonprofit organisation that works with landowners to conserve important natural areas across the state. Its work includes accepting gifts of land, financial contributions towards land value and conservation easements that place long-term protections on privately owned properties.For landowners, these arrangements offer different ways to protect places they have an interest in preserving. In some cases, ownership passes to a conservation organisation or public body. In others, an easement restricts certain forms of development or land use while allowing the property to remain privately owned.The Pascal and Ewan donations resulted in the land being transferred to county conservation, giving the 21 acres a role that combines habitat protection with public access.Iowa conservation effort protected 2,247 acres for wildlife and public accessThe two adjoining properties were among several contributions recognised by INHF for its conservation work during 2025. Over the course of the year, the foundation worked with 22 individuals, families and organisations that chose to protect land through donations of property, land value or conservation easements. Together, these contributions covered 2,247 acres spread across 15 Iowa counties. The protected areas include natural spaces that support native plants and wildlife, as well as places where residents can spend time outdoors.According to the Iowa National Heritage Foundation, the donors were recognised during a ceremony at the Iowa State Capitol on March 24. The gathering acknowledged the role of private landowners and organisations in helping secure natural areas for the future.Among the other contributions was a 52-acre donation near Rolfe in Pocahontas County, made by Fork Creek Farms, LLC and Richard C. Rastetter, Jr. The property is divided by the North Branch of Lizard Creek and includes open ground and perennial vegetation. Plans for prairie restoration are expected to improve water quality and provide feeding, resting and nesting areas for migratory birds and other wildlife.Protecting and restoring the property had been a long-standing ambition of Rastetter, who died in 2023. His family subsequently helped fulfil that plan through the contribution.Two Iowa families help secure a future for 21 acres of natural landThe 21 acres donated by the Pascal and Ewan families represent a smaller part of Iowa's wider conservation programme, but the transfer has given the adjoining properties a defined future. Their management now falls under Pocahontas County Conservation, with public recreation and wildlife habitat among the intended uses. The arrangement also illustrates how separate land donations can be combined to create a larger area for conservation.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Iraq’s al-Zaidi talks to Trump as Baghdad seeks to stay out of war on Iran
articles.summary: Call comes as Iraq’s top diplomat urges armed groups not to join any Iranian retaliation to US attacks.
articles.body:
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has told the United States that Baghdad will not let its territory be used to attack neighbouring countries, as his foreign minister warned that a new war on Iran would be a “disaster” for Iraq.

Al-Zaidi spoke to US President Donald Trump over the phone on Thursday, according to his office, as diplomatic efforts intensify to avert renewed US attacks on Iran.

The two men “discussed the evolving situation in the region, security developments, and prospects for the next phase”, al-Zaidi’s office said.

The prime minister reaffirmed Iraq’s call “for respect for the sovereignty of states and for Iraqi territory not to be used as a launching point for attacks against neighbouring countries”, it added.

He also stressed the need for diplomacy and dialogue to safeguard the region’s security and stability, it said.

Iraq, which neighbours Iran, has struggled to maintain a balancing act between US and Iranian interests since Trump launched the war on Iran in February.

Since taking office in May, al-Zaidi has prioritised the disarmament of all fighter groups in the country, including several powerful pro-Iran groups that have launched attacks in support of Iran across the region during the war.

Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein told Dijlah TV on Thursday that the potential of renewed US military attacks against Iran is “not a secret” and warned Iraqi armed groups against joining in any Iranian retaliation.

“Pushing Iraqi society into the war will lead to a disaster,” he said. “We are not prepared for war. Neither Iraqi society nor the armed forces are prepared for war.”

Hussein said Iraq had been turned into a battlefield after the US struck Iran, with the country coming under attack from both the US and Iran, as well as from armed groups inside Iraq.

“We are not part of any axis, and we do not want to let the Iraqi arena be turned into a battlefield,” he said. “We have good relations with the US and with our neighbour Iran… We need a clear policy that we are not a part of the war, and we do not want to be a part of the war.”

Since the war began, Iraq has lost more than $60bn in oil revenues, as about 90 percent of its oil exports normally pass through the Strait of Hormuz and were largely cut off when Tehran closed the waterway.

Oil accounts for about 90 percent of Iraq’s federal budget.

Since then, Iraq has been one of the few countries that have been granted exemption by Iran to pass freely through the Strait of Hormuz.

articles.title: Why one Republican won a redrawn Texas district despite blue tsunami
articles.summary: Republican redistricting largely backfired in Texas and beyond, but one redrawn district delivered for the party.
articles.body:
Dallas, Texas – Tuesday’s midterms were bruising for Republicans in Texas, a longtime right-wing stronghold.

The state elected its first Democrats to statewide office in 32 years, and the left-wing party held onto four congressional districts that were recently redesigned to favour Republicans.

But Republicans had one redistricting bright spot in a sea of unexpected defeats in Texas this midterm election cycle.

Amid the so-called blue wave, Republican Jace Yarbrough defeated Dan Barrios in Texas’s 32nd congressional district near Dallas, taking control of a heavily redrawn seat previously held by a Democrat.

Yarbrough became the only Republican this year to flip a Texas congressional seat, despite a push under United States President Donald Trump to shake up the state’s map for the right-wing party’s benefit.

So how did Yarbrough buck the trend? He was successful for two reasons, according to Matthew Wilson, a professor at Southern Methodist University who lives in the 32nd district.

“I think he did effectively pivot from a primary strategy to a general election strategy,” Wilson told Al Jazeera.

A constitutional lawyer, Yarbrough had defined his career by litigating progressive policies. But Wilson explained that the cost of living and other economic concerns took an increasingly prominent role in the final months of Yarbrough’s bid.

“In the primaries, the social issues, cultural issues were really important,” Wilson said.

“But then he pivoted very quickly and realised that those were probably not going to have the same resonance in the fall campaign. And so he did talk a lot about lowering prices. He did talk a lot about things that were of concern more to voters in the centre of the electorate.”

Wilson added there was another important factor in Yarbrough’s victory. “It was just the fact that his district was drawn to be so heavily Republican.”

The 32nd district had previously been composed of left-leaning Dallas and its immediate suburbs, but in August 2025, the Texas state legislature voted to reconfigure the congressional boundaries, with the aim of helping Republicans win five extra seats in this year’s midterms.

That push came at the behest of Trump, who called on Republican-led states across the country to follow suit.

Yarbrough’s district was redrawn to include only a portion of Dallas. It now stretches east instead, to encompass several Republican-dominated counties.

The demographics of the district also shifted dramatically.

In 2024, the district encompassed sizeable Latino, Black and Asian communities, accounting for about 60 percent of the population. The new map lowered the share of those demographics, while including several predominantly white areas.

Still, Wilson pointed out that Yarbrough’s victory was far more muted than initially expected. He won 51.5 percent of the vote to Barrios’s 48.5 percent.

“Even in his case, the race was a lot closer than he would have expected,” Wilson said. “So there was a pretty uniform Democratic swing across congressional districts.”

With the dust settling on the election, Republicans will start the next congressional term in January with 24 representatives from Texas, losing one seat to Democrats this midterm cycle.

Democrats, who will have commanding control of both chambers of Congress, will have 14 House seats filled by Texans.

The four other Democrat-held districts Texas Republicans hoped to gain via redistricting were swept up in the groundswell of opposition to Trump.

In those districts, the party’s redrawn maps largely miscalculated Latino voters, a demographic that makes up 40 percent of the state’s population and swung towards Trump in 2024, according to political experts.

This year, the demographic tilted back towards Democrats with force, fuelled both by affordability concerns and dismay over Trump’s hardline immigration policies, which disproportionately affect Latino communities.

“In political science, there’s a body of literature we call ‘group threat theory’,” Michael Adams, a professor at Texas Southern University, told Al Jazeera. “When a particular group feels that they are threatened, that mobilises them, and we normally see a higher increase in terms of voter turnout.”

One of the most resounding defeats came in the ninth congressional district in Houston, which for years encompassed an area with large Black and Latino populations. Texas’s newly redrawn map cut out some Black communities but left a large population of low-propensity Latino voters.

Democratic candidate Leticia Gutierrez ended up taking nearly 58 percent of the vote against Republican Alex Mealer.

Speaking to Al Jazeera before the election, Gutierrez said her strategy focused on reaching Latino voters through aggressive Spanish-language outreach focused on pocketbook issues.

“I always say that I have a big chunk of family that are citizens registered to vote, but if they don’t hear it in Spanish, they’re probably not going to show up,” said Gutierrez.

“I’m fortunate enough to be able to speak both languages fairly well, and so just again, doing a lot of that targeted getting out the vote, getting in front of voters, door-knocking.”

Latinos make up about 60 percent of the ninth congressional district. The demographic is even more pronounced in South Texas, where Republicans hoped to pick up the 28th, 34th and 35th districts in their redistricting push.

But in a district representing the suburbs of San Antonio, Democrat Johnny Garcia handily defeated Republican Carlos De La Cruz by more than 10 percentage points.

Along the US-Mexico border, incumbent Democrat Henry Cuellar carried his district with nearly 66 percent of the vote over Republican challenger Tano Tijerina, while in the 34th district, Representative Vicente Gonzalez skated to victory by more than 15 percentage points over Republican challenger Eric Flores.

In another border district, Tejano musician Bobby Pulido, a Democrat, unseated Republican incumbent Monica De La Cruz, whose 2022 victory presaged a wider conservative shift among Latinos in the state.

Two years later, Trump carried nearly every Latino-dominated border district in Texas, seizing on unrest over immigration policies under former President Joe Biden. He also leveraged the prevalence of conservative social views among the largely Catholic population.

The area had long been considered a Democratic stronghold.

“Democrats are very conservative here. So I’m not surprised that it went for Trump in 2024,” 37-year-old voter Donato Medina told Al Jazeera from the border city of McAllen before the vote.

“But now it’s like people are kind of waking up, because his policies are affecting them directly.”

articles.title: Former pro-democracy lawmaker sentenced to 12 1/2 years in Macao’s first national security case
articles.summary: The arrest last year of Au Kam San, 69, was the first publicly known prosecution under the Chinese territory’s national security law since it was enacted in 2009.
articles.body: HONG KONG — Macao pro-democracy former lawmaker Au Kam San was sentenced to 12 1/2 years in prison Friday in the Chinese casino hub’s first national security case following a closed-door trial that raised concerns about fairness. Au’s arrest last year was the first publicly known prosecution under Macao’s national security law since it was enacted in 2009. A Macao court found him guilty of subverting state power, breach of confidentiality and establishing contact with organizations, groups or people outside Macao to commit acts endangering national security. Au, 69, was accused of having assisted and cooperated with “hostile organizations” outside Macao for a long period of time in collecting and disseminating political views laden with ideas of subverting state power and false information, according to a court statement. Through colluding with the organizations, he was trying to incite hatred among Macao residents against the central government, with an intent to overthrow and undermine the country’s fundamental system, it said. Critics said his case reflected Beijing’s emphasis on security and intolerance of dissent, even though Macao’s pro-democracy movement has never been as influential as that in neighboring Hong Kong. Macao is a former Portuguese colony that has operated, like Hong Kong, as a special administrative region since its return to Chinese rule in 1999. It has its own political and legal systems, and Macao is the only Chinese city where casino gambling is legal. It has resorts run by affiliates of the American gaming giants MGM Resorts, Las Vegas Sands and Wynn Resorts. Au, a teacher-turned-lawmaker, served in the legislature dominated by Beijing loyalists for 20 years before stepping down in 2021. Au was also an organizer of Macao’s commemoration of the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown in Beijing. Au said he entered politics as he saw many social problems in daily life that required people to speak out. He said the Tiananmen Square pro-democracy movement in 1989 brought him and his like-minded friends together, and he later felt Macao needed people to push forward an open and democratic society. Prior to his arrest, Au was a rare voice in Macao who regularly criticized government measures and political development on Facebook and in interviews, although many considered his critiques to be mild. The court in July said Au would be represented by a court-appointed lawyer who authorities said was approved by him and that his rights were ensured by law. Au’s daughter in London, Au Hon I, previously told The Associated Press that a lawyer found by the family was not allowed to see him in prison and that her family could not speak with him for almost a year. Au’s trial was held behind closed doors in September. The court earlier said the judge decided against an open trial to ensure that national security interests would not be undermined. It came at the request of the Public Prosecutions Office and with confirmation from the city’s national security committee, which is led by Macao Chief Executive Sam Hou Fai, it said.

articles.title: Wendy's rejects a $1.4 billion takeover offer from billionaire Nelson Peltz's investor group and adopts a one-year poison pill defence, even as the struggling US burger chain closes hundreds of restaurants
articles.summary: Wendy’s has rejected a $1.4 billion takeover proposal from a group led by billionaire investor Nelson Peltz, arguing that the offer significantly
articles.body: Wendy’s has rejected a $1.4 billion takeover proposal from a group led by billionaire investor Nelson Peltz, arguing that the offer significantly undervalues the struggling burger chain and its long-term growth prospects. The US fast-food company has also adopted a one-year shareholder defence plan, commonly known as a ‘poison pill’, to make it harder for the investor group to gain greater control without board approval. The decision comes as Wendy’s battles declining sales, rising operating costs and intensifying competition, while shutting hundreds of restaurants across the country.The proposal was submitted by an investor group comprising Peltz’s Trian Fund Management, restaurant operator Flynn Group and investment firms BlueFive Capital and Sixth Street Partners. The group offered $7.35 per share in cash to acquire the shares of Wendy’s that it does not already own. The offer values the proposed acquisition at approximately $1.4 billion.Wendy’s said its independent committee of directors had unanimously rejected the unsolicited, non-binding proposal after reviewing it with independent financial and legal advisers. The committee concluded that the offer substantially undervalued the company and failed to account for the potential benefits of its new turnaround strategy, called Dave’s Way.What is Wendy’s poison pill defence?Alongside rejecting the offer, Wendy’s announced that its board had adopted a limited-duration shareholder rights plan on November 4. The arrangement is designed to discourage an investor or group from accumulating a controlling stake without offering an appropriate premium to other shareholders. Under the plan, the rights become exercisable if an individual or group acquires 15% or more of Wendy’s outstanding shares without board approval. It also applies if an existing shareholder who already owns at least 15% purchases additional shares without approval.If the threshold is triggered, other eligible shareholders will be allowed to purchase additional shares at a discounted price, potentially diluting the ownership stake of the investor that crossed the threshold. The acquiring group would not be entitled to exercise these rights. The plan will remain effective for one year and is scheduled to expire on November 3, 2027, although the board can consider ending it earlier. Wendy’s said the arrangement is intended to give its independent committee sufficient time to assess potential takeover proposals and protect the interests of all shareholders.The defence is particularly significant because Peltz’s investor group already owns approximately 16.3% of Wendy’s shares. The company also said the group had rejected an offer to enter into a customary standstill agreement, which would have restricted certain actions involving its shareholding and influence.Why is Wendy’s facing pressure?The takeover dispute comes at a difficult time for the burger chain, which has been struggling to retain customers in an increasingly competitive fast-food market. Wendy’s closed 240 restaurants in 2024 and announced earlier this year that it planned to shut as many as 358 additional outlets in 2026 as part of efforts to concentrate on more profitable locations. The company has also faced pressure from rising beef prices, ageing restaurant locations and consumers cutting back on spending. Competition from established rivals such as McDonald’s and Burger King, as well as growing burger chains including In-N-Out and Five Guys, has added to its challenges.According to market research firm Technomic, Wendy’s share of US burger-chain sales declined from 11.5% in 2019 to 10.4% in 2025. The wider fast-food industry has also experienced weaker customer traffic, particularly among lower-income consumers dealing with affordability concerns and higher household expenses. Another setback came in September, when Michigan-based Meritage Hospitality Group, one of Wendy’s largest US franchise operators, filed for bankruptcy protection after the chain attempted to terminate its franchise agreement. Meritage operates 314 Wendy’s restaurants across 15 states.New CEO bets on turnaround strategyWendy’s is attempting to reverse its declining fortunes under CEO Bob Wright, who joined the company in May. Wright is the fourth chief executive to lead the burger chain since 2024 and previously served as president and CEO of sandwich chain Potbelly. His turnaround programme, called Dave’s Way, is centred on improving food quality, strengthening marketing, simplifying restaurant operations and improving digital ordering. The strategy also aims to increase customer traffic, regain market share and improve profitability across its restaurants.Wendy’s is now testing thicker and crispier bacon, creamier Frosty desserts and whole-leaf lettuce in its sandwiches. It is also removing lower-selling menu items to simplify kitchen operations and allowing franchisees to make breakfast optional so they can concentrate on more profitable meal periods. Its independent committee has backed Wright's leadership, saying the proposed acquisition does not reflect the value that could be generated through the execution of Dave’s Way.However, its latest financial performance shows the scale of the challenge. Wendy’s reported revenue of $547 million for the July-September quarter, exceeding analysts' expectations of $531 million. Its same-store sales, which measure sales at restaurants operating for at least a year, declined 5.2%. Although the decline was smaller than the 6.4% analysts had anticipated, it highlighted the continuing difficulty of bringing customers back.Peltz's long association with Wendy’sThe takeover proposal also carries significance because Peltz is not a newcomer to Wendy’s. The billionaire investor previously served as chairman of the company's board for 17 years, stepping down in 2024. His son, Bradley Peltz, continues to serve on Wendy’s board and is also a franchisee.Peltz had explored the possibility of taking Wendy’s private in 2022 but abandoned those plans in January 2023, citing improvements in the company's business momentum at the time. His latest proposal comes as the chain faces renewed financial and operational challenges.Founded in 1969 by Dave Thomas, Wendy’s built its reputation around square-shaped hamburgers, its Frosty desserts and the iconic 'Where's the beef?' advertising campaign of the 1980s. The company had 5,969 restaurants in the US and another 1,428 outlets across 38 countries at the end of 2025.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Colorado police officer killed, 3 more officers wounded after suspect opens fire near bus
articles.summary: A suspect trying to board an RTD bus near Denver opened fire on Lakewood police officers, killing one and wounding three others Thursday evening.
articles.body: A Colorado police officer was killed and three more officers were wounded in a shooting Thursday evening near a bus outside Denver, authorities said. Lakewood police said officers responded to a report of a suspicious person near the intersection of Colfax Avenue and Wadsworth Boulevard around 6:30 p.m., where they encountered a suspect attempting to board a bus. The suspect opened fire on officers, striking four of them, Lakewood Police Public Information Officer John Romero said during a news conference. "We are very sorry to report that one of those agents has been pronounced dead of their injuries," Romero said. FOUR DEAD, INCLUDING WASHINGTON DEPUTY, FOLLOWING DOMESTIC CALL SHOOTING; ANOTHER DEPUTY ON LIFE SUPPORT The suspect was shot by police and pronounced dead at the scene, Romero said. A civilian was also injured and transported to a local hospital. Police did not immediately provide details about the extent of the injuries or the conditions of the three surviving officers. Authorities said the suspect was attempting to board a Regional Transportation District (RTD) bus when officers approached. CHICAGO HOSPITAL SHOOTING LEAVES 1 OFFICER DEAD, OTHER 'FIGHTING FOR HIS LIFE'; SUSPECT IN CUSTODY "Within seconds of agents approaching the suspect, the suspect opened fire on our agents," Romero said. Romero also delivered an emotional message to the fallen officer's family: "We just want the family to know that we love them, that we're here for them, and Lakewood Police Department is a family, and we will be here for each other." Colorado Gov. Jared Polis released a statement following the deadly shooting. "Law enforcement put their lives on the line for our safety everyday and I am heartbroken to learn that a Lakewood Police Agent was killed in the line of duty this evening," Polis wrote. "My heart goes out to their family and friends," he continued. "My thoughts are also with the three agents who are still receiving care at area hospitals, as well as the civilian who was wounded, and I wish them a full and speedy recovery. Thank you to law enforcement who run into danger to keep us safe and to protect our communities." Polis said the Colorado State Patrol was assisting at the scene and participating in a procession from the hospital honoring the fallen officer. articles.title: Home Office investigation after BBC catches lawyer offering to make fines go away
articles.summary: The Home Office said it will be investigating the allegations to see whether there has been a breach of immigration rules.
articles.body:
The Home Office has launched an investigation after a solicitor was secretly filmed by the BBC explaining how he could make a £45,000 illegal-working fine go away.

Mohammad Alias Yousaf - also known as Alias - made the claim to an undercover reporter, who was posing as a mini-mart owner facing a fine for employing an illegal worker.

The Solicitors Regulation Authority has said it will also examine the BBC's findings to see whether there has been misconduct by solicitors or law firms.

The Bradford-based solicitor told his potential client he could avoid paying the fine if he was able to find someone overseas prepared to declare themselves the owner of the mini-mart.

Yousaf has denied ever providing such advice to anyone, or giving false information to the Home Office.

The BBC's wider investigation also revealed at least £150m is currently owed to the government in uncollected illegal-working fines, according to Home Office figures exclusively obtained by the BBC.

In response, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood ordered a review of the way such fines are issued and collected.

Mahmood said she wanted to thank the BBC "for exposing those who undermine our rules".

"Illegal working undermines honest employers, undercuts local wages, and fuels organised immigration crime," she added.

The Home Office said it would be investigating the allegations to see whether there had been a breach of immigration rules.

Senior politicians have since called UK immigration enforcement "weak" and a "laughing stock".

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp has called for Yousaf to be "struck off as a solicitor", while shadow justice minister Nick Timothy has written to the head of the regulator for solicitors to take "urgent action, and stop Mr Yousaf practising as a solicitor".

Philp said: "Shabana Mahmood likes to boast about how many fines are issued, but now it turns out most just get ignored. No wonder we have a borders crisis with enforcement turning into a laughing stock."

A spokesman for the Solicitors Regulation Authority said: "We will be considering this information to see if there are any issues arising which we need to look into further."

The BBC also heard from a law enforcement whistleblower who, speaking anonymously, revealed it was a struggle to identify the real owners of businesses caught with illegal workers.

She said she had seen immigration fine notices, "some worth £40,000, stuffed in a box" on a mini-mart counter.

"I've said to owners 'I see you've got a fine, are you going to pay it?' And they just laugh in my face, throw the fine back in a box and say 'it's got nothing to do with me'."

Over the past 18 months, the BBC has carried out a wider probe into illegal working and criminality linked to some High Street businesses, including mini-marts and barbershops.

Our undercover reporter, who pretended to have a £45,000 illegal working fine, secretly recorded Yousaf saying he could transfer the penalty into someone else's name for a fee of £4,500.

Yousaf has denied ever advising anyone to put a penalty into the name of someone who was not responsible for a business, or to give false information to the Home Office, and said he never would.

"My work is to challenge penalties lawfully, through the routes Parliament has provided, usually on the basis that the person found was not an employee at all," Yousaf told the BBC.

He added that when our reporter proposed putting his business into someone else's name, Yousaf had told him in writing he could not advance an untruthful or dishonest case and did not act for him.

The government said "arrests and raids are at their highest ever levels and removals of illegal workers up 50%".

articles.title: US Justice Department sues Penn State over undocumented students’ tuition
articles.summary: The lawsuit challenges Penn State’s policy that allows undocumented students to qualify for reduced tuition rates.
articles.body:
The United States Department of Justice has sued Pennsylvania State University, accusing the institution of violating federal law by offering in-state tuition rates to undocumented students while denying the same reduced rates to all US citizens.

The lawsuit , filed on Thursday, argues that the university’s tuition policy discriminates against citizens.

Currently, undocumented students can qualify for in-state tuition if they meet Penn State’s residency standards.

But prosecutors have rejected that policy, saying it violates a federal law that bars “preferential treatment” in higher education for undocumented immigrants, unless the same benefits are available to US citizens.

In the US, public universities typically charge lower tuition to students who are residents of the state where the institution is located, while students from other states pay higher rates.

Proponents of such policies say in-state tuition helps prevent “brain drain”, wherein students might leave the state to attend universities elsewhere. They also reward residents of the state, who contribute taxes to the education system.

Advocates argue the same benefits should be directed towards undocumented students, who are often brought to the country as minors. Making undocumented students eligible for in-state tuition can also reduce the barriers they face to education.

But the Justice Department is seeking a court order preventing Penn State from continuing to offer in-state tuition rates to undocumented students, including those living in Pennsylvania, regardless of their immigration status.

It is also seeking to block the university from adopting future tuition policies that give undocumented students “preferential treatment” over US citizens.

“Congress made a deliberate policy choice that states and their public institutions may not grant tuition benefits to illegal aliens unless those same benefits are made to all US citizens,” Brett Shumate, assistant attorney general of the Justice Department’s Civil Division, said in a statement.

The lawsuit is part of a broader campaign under President Donald Trump to challenge state policies granting reduced tuition to undocumented students.

Since returning to office for a second term in 2025, Trump has sought to clamp down on undocumented immigration, promising to lead the largest deportation effort in US history.

The Justice Department said Thursday’s filing brings the total number of lawsuits it has brought challenging such policies to 27. It also said six cases in Texas, Kentucky, Oklahoma, Nebraska, Illinois and Kansas resulted in court orders permanently blocking similar tuition policies.

In Thursday’s lawsuit, prosecutors called such policies unconstitutional. They also argued that laws like the 1996 Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act ban “public benefits from serving as an incentive” for undocumented immigration.

“Federal law prohibits illegal aliens from being eligible to receive postsecondary education benefits based on residence within a state if such benefits are denied to US citizens residing in other states,” the lawsuit said.

“There are no exceptions. Yet, Pennsylvania State University has ignored this congressional prohibition.”

According to Penn State’s current residency requirements, non-citizen applicants must have attended an accredited Pennsylvania high school for at least four years and graduated from one to qualify for in-state tuition.

Penn State said it was aware of the complaint and was reviewing it.

articles.title: A wildfire killed their loved ones in Spain. These British families demand to know why
articles.summary: Nine British nationals were among the 15 people who died when fire ripped through the village of Bédar this summer.
articles.body:
Relatives of Britons killed in this summer's wildfires in Spain have told the BBC they are disgusted, after regional politicians blocked an official inquiry into the disaster.

Nine British nationals were among the 15 people who died when fire ripped through the hillside village of Bédar, in the province of Almería in south-eastern Spain, on 9 July.

Families have criticised the authorities' actions, including the decision not to send an emergency alert to mobile phones as the flames closed in.

"If that evacuation warning had come through in time, my father would still be alive," says Duncan Chard, who blames failures by officials on the day for a number of the deaths.

He lost his father Michael and his dad's partner Christine.

The governing People's Party (PP) and far-right Vox in the Andalusian parliament have rejected a request for a commission of inquiry made by the opposition Socialist party to which Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez belongs.

The PP and Vox argued that an ongoing criminal investigation would provide the necessary answers.

The Andalusian government, PP and Vox have been approached for comment.

Families of those killed say there must be a public and transparent probe.

"It's just outrageous. It's an injustice. As family members, we're absolutely disgusted. This is an insult," says Duncan Chard.

The families also say their grief has been made worse by how police have handled their loved ones' remains and belongings since the fire.

Michael Chard built his house in Bédar from scratch. "He called it Casa Micas," his son said. "It was his place in the sun, it was his little paradise."

On the morning of the fire, Michael's partner Christine had met friends and was due to go to the hairdresser. "Then everything changed... the whole world changed for them," he said.

Duncan Chard said his father, who had two artificial knees and walked with a stick, left his house with Christine as soon as they saw the flames. They left their phones and passports behind and tried to escape by car, but the road was blocked.

"This is an action of a brave person who was fighting to the end," he said.

Andalusia's emergencies chief, Antonio Sanz, has said the region decided not to use the system that sends emergency alerts to mobile phones because it could not be tailored to specific communities.

Officials have said some residents needed to evacuate while others were safer staying in their homes. They also argued an alert could have caused panic and traffic jams.

"Issue the damned alert!" said Chard. "Ring the bells, send the police guy out with his horn, go door to door, do everything."

Thomas-Wolf Verdonckt, a Belgian virologist whose father Stanislas, 63, died, was on the phone to him as the flames approached.

He says the victims "never received advice on what they should do, and certainly not warnings that they were in danger", and that the authorities' claim that everyone in the area was given adequate warning is not true.

"The only contact that the government managed to make with the victims was a couple of minutes before the flames engulfed everyone. One police car drove by with the sirens on. There was no talking, there was no messaging."

Bédar's emergency plan was last approved in 2019, and regional officials say it was in the process of being updated. The municipality is classified by the Andalusian government as being at risk from wildfires.

Of the 15 people who died in Bédar, 14 were foreign nationals: nine British citizens, three Belgian, one French and one American. The other victim was Spanish.

In the days after the fire, Sanz faced a backlash for appearing to blame the victims. He said some people who made the decision to leave "at the last minute, took the wrong path".

Verdonckt has been trying to find answers ever since the blaze.

"The morning afterwards, the Spanish officials brought out... a version of events which was simply the complete opposite of what I experienced," he said.

He also believes a public inquiry is needed to prevent a similar disaster happening in Spain in the future.

"They are putting the safety of citizens in second place. That's simply not okay."

Danni Gillam-Kirton, an assistant headteacher from Nottinghamshire, lost her parents Pete and Fran in the fire.

They had lived in Bédar since 2018. Fran, a former headteacher, ran a quiz night that raised money for the local school and church.

"They were fantastic parents, my biggest champions and cheerleaders," said Danni. "They leave a huge, huge hole in our lives."

She says her mother texted her at about 19:00 to say they had packed in case they had to leave.

"They were waiting for instructions, and those instructions didn't come," she said.

Her parents died on the part of Bédar known as English Hill, one of the places where, families say, the authorities' only contact came minutes before the flames arrived.

Gillam-Kirton says her grief has been made worse by the way the Spanish authorities have behaved since.

Local police had told the family that Pete and Fran's car had been "meticulously searched" by forensic specialists and that she would find nothing.

But in August, a month afterwards, Gillam-Kirton and her husband found what appeared to be human bones in the burnt-out car in which her father died. "I picked up what I recognised to be... part of a pelvis or a hip joint," she said.

Gillam-Kirton fears they were her father's remains.

Within minutes they also found her parents' mobile phones, jewellery, house keys and money. Police had earlier told the family that no personal belongings had survived.

Spain's Guardia Civil police have been approached for comment.

The fragments were eventually sent to Madrid for testing. The family says police have now told them no DNA was recovered and that the bones were those of an animal.

But Gillam-Kirton says experts, including a forensic anthropologist who worked on the Grenfell Tower fire investigation, believe the fragments were human.

"We still don't know who or what they are," she said.

Gillam-Kirton complained to the Guardia Civil. She says the reply told her only that the matter had been passed to the courts, and offered condolences for "the death of your relative", in the singular, when in fact she had lost both her parents.

"It feels like they're going to hope that we exhaust ourselves," she said. "Either the burden of grief is going to be enough for us to give up, or that we're going to financially exhaust ourselves."

Gillam-Kirton says there is "a real lack of empathy when you're dealing with families that have lost so much".

The one thing she wants above all is for someone to acknowledge what went wrong: "No-one seems to be willing to say 'do you know what, we made a mistake and for that we are sorry'."

The death toll in Bédar was the highest from any single fire in Spain during the summer of 2026, and one of the largest in the country's history.

Many victims were trapped as they tried to escape the village, as survivor Malcolm Timbrell told me outside his devastated home in July.

The cause of the disaster, also known as the Los Gallardos fire after the neighbouring town where it started, is the subject of a criminal investigation.

In July, the Guardia Civil said it was believed to have been started by a fallen power line, but that explanation has been called into question.

The BBC has seen a letter in which the Andalusian government refused a request from Socialist MPs for its official reports on the fire. These included any documents explaining why no alert was sent to mobile phones.

The letter, signed by Sanz in September, said the documents could not be released because the criminal investigation is under secreto de sumario , a court order keeping the case file confidential.

Gillam-Kirton says the criminal case is focused on how the fire started, and that it will not necessarily examine the emergency response unless families pay lawyers to put that evidence before the judge.

"How can you have faith in these measures that they're putting in to mitigate future disasters if you don't know fully what happened the first time around?" she said.

"That's why you have a public inquiry," said Duncan Chard, "because the public need answers."

Families in the UK, Belgium and Spain have set up various support groups, as well as a website called helpbedar.com.

They have launched an appeal to pay for legal action, aiming to raise €100,000 (£83,000). Fundraising events are being held in both Spain and the UK, and so far about €11,000 has been collected.

Relatives say their fight is like David and Goliath.

"We are getting steamrolled by the Andalusian government," said Chard.

Ultimately, the families say all they want is answers, and for lessons to be learned so that others do not suffer the same ordeal.

They say they want their fight to be a tribute to their loved ones who died.

"I feel like this is all I can do for them," said Gillam-Kirton.

articles.title: Lottie Brooks book success makes Hove author 'grateful'
articles.summary: Katie Kirby, from, Hove is releasing the 10th book in the successful children's series.
articles.body:
The best-selling author of the popular Lottie Brooks series of children's books says writing them has been "lots of fun to do".

Katie Kirby, from Hove, has sold three million copies in five years.

The tenth in the series, Lottie Brooks's Twelve Disasters of Christmas, has just been released.

Kirby, who illustrates the books herself, said: "I feel really grateful that so many people love to read about Lottie's life and I get to write it for my job."

She added: "Lottie is a naturally, clumsy and chaotic character who is always going through lots of disasters.

"She's just a real, everyday girl going through all the things we all go through - growing up, going to a new school, going through puberty.

"I'm writing about how she gets through it all and tries to be a better person.

"But they're all happy tales essentially."

Kirby previously worked in advertising, and started writing a blog when she had a baby and toddler at home.

"That led to three adult books - and then people said my sense of humour and style would work well for children," she said.

"I wrote the first Lottie book as something I would have loved to have read when I was that age.

"Everybody can see a bit of themselves in Lottie."

Kirby said the new book is written as a collection of short stories, rather than a diary.

articles.title: Why is Iran exempting India, China, Qatar, Iraq from Hormuz restrictions?
articles.summary: Tehran says ships from four countries can cross Hormuz freely, but analysts say the deals carry political risks.
articles.body:
Iran has exempted ships from India, China, Iraq and Qatar from its Strait of Hormuz restrictions, a senior Iranian lawmaker said on Tuesday.

“Ships from these countries pass freely, and the Americans do not intercept them either,” Amir Hayat Moqaddam, deputy chairman of the Iranian parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, told the Iranian Students’ News Agency (ISNA).

Iran effectively shut the strait early in the US-Israel war on Iran , which began on February 28, and the United States reimposed a naval blockade on Iran’s southern ports in July.

So why have these four countries been granted passage through the critical strait, and can their ships really sail freely while the blockade remains in place?

What does Iran get in return for letting ships pass?

It will receive medicine from India and political backing from China, according to Hayat Moqaddam. Iran already receives diplomatic support from Qatar, which is leading mediation efforts to end the US-Israel war on Iran.

Hayat Moqaddam said Tehran will also collect transit fees from Indian and Chinese ships, while Qatari vessels pass free. He did not say whether Iraqi ships will pay a toll.

“Whatever the lawmaker says is the rationale – the big question is if it works and, if yes, to what extent?” Rouzbeh Parsi, an Iran analyst and affiliated researcher at Lund University’s Department of History and Human Rights Studies, told Al Jazeera.

“Iran has been under sanctions for a very long time, so bartering and quid pro quos in trade are nothing new,” he said. The difference now, he added, is that “it’s about poking holes in an embargo and getting crucial goods/services in and out”.

Nader Hashemi, an associate professor of Middle East politics at Georgetown University, said that “most likely Iran is charging a transit fee or a percentage of the cargo value to allow those ships to go through without being harassed”.

“It’s a clever move by Tehran for several reasons,” Wolfgang Pusztai, a security and defence analyst and Austria’s former defence attache to Libya, told Al Jazeera.

“If successful, this move will generate significant revenue for Iran, as China is by far the largest purchaser of Iranian crude oil, buying nearly 90 percent of Iran’s total oil exports,” he said.

By including Qatar, with its many liquefied natural gas (LNG) buyers, and India, Iran is also “trying to undermine acceptance” of Washington’s strategy in the conflict, especially as it charges Qatar no tolls, he added.

Why does it matter to these four countries?

All four are highly dependent on the Strait of Hormuz for exports.

Of the 10.23 million barrels a day of Gulf crude that passed through the strait in October, about 42 percent went to China and 13 percent to India, Muyu Xu, a senior crude oil analyst at the analytics firm Kpler, told Al Jazeera.

“China is the country most able to cross US interests. The question is whether Beijing considers it worth the potential political cost,” Parsi said.

Asia is particularly reliant on Gulf oil and gas usually shipped out via Hormuz. Countries there have much to offer in return for allowing ships to pass.

“For India, the shutdown of oil from the Gulf has been a great loss – and it is a big producer of the pharmaceuticals that Iran cannot manufacture itself,” he said.

Qatar, which is mediating between Washington and Tehran, shipped no LNG through the strait in August, but managed 1.8 million tonnes in October, Xu said.

Its crude transits fell over the same period, from 517,000 barrels a day to 193,000, while Iraq’s rose from 1.69 million to 2.65 million.

Kpler has been unable to trace the origin of up to two million barrels a day of Middle Eastern crude, so both countries’ flows may be higher, Xu said.

“India and Qatar have closer relationships with DC they need to maintain – while both of them also feel let down by Trump,” Parsi said, adding, “For Qatar, maintaining a relationship with Iran is also vital since it’s an unavoidable neighbour.”

“So for all of them, there are upsides for these exemptions from Iranian restrictions but also political dangers,” he said.

Iran began letting some vessels from countries it considers friendly pass within weeks of the war starting. And in April, its military command said “brotherly” Iraq was exempt.

With the Iraqi exemption, Iran “probably intends to support the economic recovery” of its western neighbour, a fellow Shia-majority country, Pusztai said.

Will ships be able to get past the US blockade?

US Central Command (CENTCOM) has said the blockade applies to “all vessels of all nations entering or leaving coastal areas or ports in Iran”, while vessels avoiding Iranian ports are not affected.

It has also said humanitarian shipments, including “food and medical supplies essential for the survival of the civilian populations”, can pass after inspection.

But Hayat Moqaddam did not appear to limit the exemptions to ships trading with other Gulf states, Pusztai noted. “If this is really the case, this would also have a significant impact on the other Gulf states, including Saudi Arabia,” he said.

“This could make the continuation of the American naval blockade more difficult and less effective, assuming Washington accepts this Iranian move,” he said. The main change, he added, is that the exemption “would also cover Chinese/Indian ships from/to Iran”, if the US accepts it.

It is also unclear whether “ships of these countries” means the flag a vessel flies, its owner, its operator or some other link, Pusztai said.

Ending the blockade is one of Tehran’s demands before it will commit to broader peace talks with the US, which will include discussions about Iran’s nuclear programme. Qatar-mediated talks currently centre on an Iranian proposal to reopen the strait if the US meets seven conditions, including this and lifting sanctions.

“It seems to be that Iran tries to separate the questions of free passage through the Strait of Hormuz and oil exports from the nuclear question,” Pusztai said, adding, “The American reaction will show if this is successful.”

Will this make a difference to oil markets?

“I think they make only limited difference at present,” Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG Group, told Al Jazeera.

“Markets are back to pricing in a peace deal, but if conflict flares up at full tilt, then Iranian commanders may not have time to distinguish their targets,” he said, adding: “At present, the focus remains squarely on the prospects of a broader deal.”

An exemption has not guaranteed safety. On October 30, the Qatari LNG carrier Al Mayeda was struck by “unidentified objects” in the Gulf, said its owner, Qatar Gas Transport Company.

More than 120 commercial ships have been hit in the region since the war began, with October being the worst month, according to data from the International Maritime Organization and United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations.
