articles.title: 'Misleading' student loans information left out examples of higher-salary repayments
articles.summary: The Treasury Committee chair says she is "shocked" after one university compared repayments to the price of coffee.
articles.body:
Several universities in England have only been using below-average salaries in examples of student loan repayments on their websites, the BBC has found.

Treasury Committee chair Dame Meg Hillier, who led a recent inquiry into student loans, said some information about repayments was "misleading", including one instance where they were compared to the "cost of a daily coffee".

She also said the Department for Education (DfE) must include higher-salary examples on its own website, too.

The DfE said it would review the information it provides, while universities said their websites referred to government information and would be reviewed where necessary.

Student loan repayments are tied to earnings, so the more you earn, the more you repay every month - and graduates generally go on to earn more than non-graduates.

Current and prospective students in England take out Plan 5 loans to pay for their tuition fees and living costs. They repay 9% of anything they earn over £25,000 for 40 years, or until the loan is paid off.

The BBC looked at publicly available information on more than 110 university websites in England and found cases of inaccurate information about the salary at which they start repaying and the length of time they repay for.

It also found that 12 universities only gave students worked examples of repayments based on earnings that are less than the UK average, which is £39,039.

How student loans work for tuition fees and living costs

Three friends on their student debt: One paid off, one chipping away and one creeping up

Student loan terms to be made clearer in England

The University of Gloucestershire website, for example, specified a £26,000 salary would mean repaying £7.47 per month, while Northumbria University and the University of Huddersfield gave examples of £75 monthly repayments based on a £35,000 salary.

Northumbria University's website said those graduates would be "repaying an amount less than the cost of a daily coffee" - a comparison that has been removed since the university was contacted by the BBC.

The DfE website also only gives examples of monthly repayments for people earning up to £38,400 on other student loan plans, but does not include any real-world repayment examples for Plan 5 students.

Repayments are 9% of earnings over £25,000, so someone earning £30,000 will repay £37.50 per month, but someone earning £100,000 will repay £562.50 per month.

Megan Russon, 21, is a recently graduated tax accountant from Cannock with a starting salary of around £29,000, meaning she will repay about £30 a month.

However, she expects to earn around £50,000 when she becomes chartered in three years' time, and will be repaying about £187 per month.

Megan says universities gave examples of repayments based on earnings of between £25,000 and £45,000 at open days and said graduates "wouldn't even notice the repayments because they should be minimal".

"At the time, I wasn't sure what salary I was even going to be on when I graduated," she said.

"When I was at university, I started realising the salaries that I was going to be on after I graduated, then I started realising actually this is going to be impacting me quite a lot."

The BBC's analysis found most university websites did not give worked examples, and most also referred to DfE, Student Loans Company or Student Finance England information whether they did or not.

More than a dozen provided examples of repayments based on higher-than-average earnings, but 12 gave examples that were lower:

University of Gloucestershire (repaying £7.50 per month)

University of Birmingham (repaying £22 per month)

London South Bank University (repaying £22.50 per month)

Manchester Metropolitan University (repaying £33 per month)

Birmingham City University, Open University, the University of Sheffield, and the University of Wolverhampton (repaying £37.50 per month)

University of Portsmouth (repaying £45 per month)

Birkbeck University (repaying £54 per month)

Northumbria University and University of Huddersfield (repaying £75 per month)

There were also instances of inaccurate information. The University of Exeter said Plan 5 loans were written off a decade earlier than they actually are, Royal Holloway and Edge Hill listed the wrong repayment thresholds, and Harper Adams said students from England were still on Plan 2 loans. All four universities have updated their websites since being contacted by the BBC.

"I'm pretty shocked at what the BBC has uncovered here and I'm going to be raising it with the relevant MPs and urging them to write to the universities in their constituencies to make them step up and do a better job," Dame Meg said.

She said the DfE should be "taking the lead" by reflecting repayments for higher earners, but that universities also "have a responsibility to the young people that they're taking on board for the three or four years of their degree".

Dame Meg chaired an inquiry into student loans this year and said the DfE had been "mis-selling" Plan 2 loans , which were given between 2012 and 2023 in England and are still issued in Wales.

Her report said the DfE had not made clear how higher earnings would affect monthly repayments and criticised comparisons to £30-a-month phone contracts.

The DfE then pledged to "improve the current information that is provided to prospective borrowers" including "the impact of salary progression" on monthly repayments.

Phone contract comparisons 'amounted to mis-selling' student loans, MPs say

Student loans inquiry finds many did not understand terms

'Deeply misleading' school talks compared student loans to £30 phone contracts

The DfE said its guidance sets out "how repayments are calculated across the different repayment plans", adding that it was "vital" that university applicants have "clear and accurate information".

"We have committed to reviewing the information we provide following the Treasury Committee's recommendations, and we will. We are also working with universities to ensure the information they provide to students is clear and up to date," it added.

The University of Gloucestershire, the University of Birmingham and Harper Adams University said they had updated their websites and Birkbeck, University of London said it was reviewing the information.

The University of Sheffield said its example was illustrative, while Manchester Metropolitan University and the University of Wolverhampton said examples were explanatory and would be reviewed. London South Bank University said it regularly reviews content on its website to ensure it is helpful and accurate.

The Open University said it gave examples of "income levels that are most likely to reflect our students' circumstances", although many students "go on to earn significantly more", while the University of Portsmouth said its example was taken from Student Finance England and would be updated to "reflect the most recent average salary".

Northumbria University said its example of £35,000 was "broadly in line with the average for full-time workers in the North East of England" but added: "We recognise that higher earners will make higher monthly repayments and will further review all pages to make sure the wording is as clear and precise as possible."

Birmingham City University declined to comment. The BBC has requested a comment from the University of Huddersfield.

articles.title: Sunderland project using AI to help eye tests detect diabetes
articles.summary: Researchers hope the technology will allow for a quicker diagnosis for patients.
articles.body:
AI will be used in routine eye scans as part of a scheme to detect early signs of illnesses such as heart disease and diabetes.

The Northern Ophthalmic Research and Innovation (NORI) hub at Sunderland University has received £12.2m from the government through UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) for the project in the hope of diagnosing patients quicker.

Matthew Campbell, interim pro vice-chancellor for health and co-director of NORI, said the money would help the team develop the technology and take it into international markets.

While the tool will initially focus on diabetes and cardiovascular disease, the approach could later be expanded to dementia and strokes.

NORI is one of five new UKRI-backed healthcare hubs using technology to diagnose illnesses.

The other hubs are in Exeter, Southampton and London, which all focus on developing high tech tools.

Science minister Chris McDonald, who visited NORI on Thursday, said he hoped the funding would help patients access treatment quicker.

He said: "Earlier diagnosis means better outcomes for patients and less pressure on our NHS, and technology has a vital role to play."

The technology will use the tiny blood vessels and nerve tissue at the back of the eye, which NORI said can reveal clues about a person's wider health before symptoms appear.

AI will be used to analyse the routine eye scans alongside NHS health records and community data to identify subtle changes which may signal early signs of disease.

Campbell said: "This investment creates a new health innovation ecosystem for the North East.

"We now have the scale to develop technologies, test them in real-world healthcare settings and take them into national and international markets."

articles.title: Bristol then and now: The Old Vic, SS Great Britain and Blitz
articles.summary: An interactive gallery showing how Bristol has changed over the past century.
articles.body:
In the third of our interactive galleries showing how Bristol has changed over the years, we take a wander down King Street to see how this thriving night-time destination used to look.

Not far away is Wine Street, one of many city centre areas destroyed and rebuilt after heavy German bombing in 1940.

Swipe left and right to reveal how each location has changed over the decades.

Taken in the 1880s, this photograph of King Street shows the Coopers Hall, the Theatre Royal/Bristol Old Vic and the St Nicholas' Almshouses. As Bristolians will tell you, Bristol Old Vic is the oldest continually-used theatre in the English-speaking world, and remains at the heart of King Street – now one of the hubs of the city's nightlife.

Every so often you come across an image that shows in the starkest terms how the air raids of the Second World War altered Bristol beyond recognition. This is Wine Street, after incendiary devices were dropped over 24-25 November 1940. Much of what was the city centre, sitting on what is now Castle Park, was destroyed. Once again, the clue to it being the same scene is a church spire - this time Christ Church with St Ewen.

The SS Great Britain may be one of Bristol's most popular attractions now, but she was in a sorry state when she returned up the River Avon in 1970 as thousands of people watched from the banks. Having been used for coal storage in the Falkland Islands and abandoned as a rotting hulk, years of painstaking work restored her to her former glory.

articles.title: Trump’s 250-foot triumphal arch in Washington halted by federal judge
articles.summary: A federal judge late Thursday temporarily halted the Trump administration's plans to begin construction of president Donald Trump's proposed triumphal
articles.body: A federal judge late Thursday temporarily halted the Trump administration's plans to begin construction of president Donald Trump's proposed triumphal arch in Washington, siding with Vietnam war veterans, the district of columbia and Virginia, who have challenged the project in court.US district judge Tanya Chutkan issued a temporary restraining order barring the government from undertaking any construction-related work at the proposed site for 14 days while legal proceedings continue. She said a detailed explanation of her decision would be provided in a subsequent opinion, according to CBS news.The order came shortly after the National capital planning commission (NCPC) approved the design and construction plans for the proposed 250-foot monument. The arch is planned for a site between the Lincoln memorial and Arlington national cemetery.The NCPC, the federal agency responsible for overseeing planning and development in the region, voted 8-4 in favour of the project following nearly nine hours of public testimony from lawmakers, veterans, architects and residents of Washington and Virginia. The commission includes several officials appointed by or associated with Trump.Despite the court's intervention, the exact timeline for the construction remains uncertain. The justice department had informed the court last month that work could begin as early as Thursday.In a separate court filing on Wednesday night, the Trump administration said a construction company might be making preliminary arrangements away from the site in anticipation of receiving the necessary permits.Before the commission meeting, its executive director, Mark Paoletta, recommended approval of the final site and building plans for the monument, which is intended to commemorate 250 years of American independence.Paoletta, who also serves as the chief lawyer at the Office of Management and Budget, praised Trump's vision for the project, describing it as a historic initiative and claiming it would become the “grandest arch ever built by mankind”.However, California representative Jared Huffman, the top democrat on the house natural resources committee, strongly opposed the proposal during the hearing, calling it illegal and warning that it would undermine the symbolic connection between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington national cemetery.“This arch would dishonour America, our ideals, and our laws,” Huffman said, arguing that Congress should be responsible for debating and deciding on the proposed monument.Marine veteran Jimi Shaughnessy also criticised the design, saying a massive structure surrounded by tourists, food trucks and buses would be disrespectful to fallen service members and their families.He further accused the administration of prioritising an unwanted monument over issues affecting military families and using taxpayer money to advance the project while disregarding legal and regulatory requirements.Details of Trump's proposed triumphal archAccording to documents submitted to the NCPC, the main structure will stand 166 feet tall and feature three gilded figures at its summit. The central sculpture will depict a golden, winged female figure, flanked by a golden flying eagle on either side, taking the monument's overall height to 250 feet.The proposed site is close to Ronald Reagan Washington national Airport. However, the federal aviation administration has determined that the structure would not pose a threat to air navigation. Its assessment includes safety requirements involving warning lights, a non-standard eternal flame and continuous floodlighting.The monument will also have an observation deck. The Trump administration estimates that it could attract between 2,000 and 22,400 visitors daily.Construction is expected to take approximately three years. The arch will be located at the centre of memorial circle, across the Potomac River from the Lincoln Memorial.However, the overall project cost and its funding arrangements have not yet been disclosed.Trump had described his proposed triumphal arch in September as a “top grade Military Complex”, suggesting that it would accommodate drones and sniper ammunition. However, the plans submitted to the planning commission do not mention these proposed military facilities.During a court hearing in October, Justice Department lawyers declined to provide further details about the national security features of the proposed structure.The NCPC said it had received more than 1,300 public comments on the project, with the overwhelming majority opposing the proposal.Why the project is facing legal challengesThe commission's approval came as Judge Chutkan was considering requests to prevent the administration from moving ahead with construction.A group of Vietnam War veterans, along with the commonwealth of Virginia and Washington, DC, have filed separate lawsuits arguing that the administration is proceeding without the necessary congressional authorisation and has failed to follow the required legal procedures.In an order issued on Tuesday, Chutkan directed the government to inform her within an hour of any decision by the NCPC. She also required a 30-minute advance notice of any preparations for construction, allowing her sufficient time to consider whether a halt was necessary.After receiving the notifications late Thursday, the judge issued the temporary restraining order prohibiting construction, excavation, demolition, land disturbance, utility installation, road closures and other related activities at the site for 14 days.During a hearing last month, Chutkan indicated that a central question in the case was whether the Vietnam War veterans had the legal standing to challenge the project.Earlier this year, the US Supreme Court ruled that plaintiffs in a similar case challenging the construction of a White House ballroom were unlikely to have the legal standing required to bring the lawsuit.The Justice Department has urged Chutkan to follow the supreme court's reasoning, describing the objections raised by the plaintiffs as “breathless”. Lawyers representing the veterans and other groups, however, have argued that their case involves different legal issues and have pressed the judge to stop construction.Two Vietnam war veterans involved in the case, Michael Lemmon and Shaun Byrnes, told the court last month that the proposed monument would adversely affect their visits to graves at Arlington national cemetery. They argued that its enormous size and intended purpose would diminish their experience at the cemetery.In a separate lawsuit filed in late October, Virginia and Washington, DC, also challenged the project. The case was assigned to Chutkan, who had heard arguments from the veterans a day earlier.The attorneys general representing the two jurisdictions warned that beginning construction would cause irreparable damage. They argued that the project could create severe traffic congestion between the neighbouring jurisdictions, increase pollution and stormwater runoff in the Potomac River, disrupt emergency services and create several other administrative and environmental difficulties.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'The veil of shame around postnatal depression needs to go'
articles.summary: Mums are helping other parents to recognise the signs of postnatal depression and psychosis.
articles.body:
"Women, since the beginning of time, have birthed and looked after children and I just couldn't be bothered. I thought I was lazy."

Those are the words of Laura, 45, from Cheltenham, in Gloucestershire, who weeks after undergoing an emergency Caesarean section struggled so much with postnatal depression that she needed psychiatric care.

The NHS says postnatal depression , also known as postpartum depression, is a "common" mental health condition that can happen after having a baby.

"Postnatal depression can happen to anyone and this is why the veil of shame needs to come down, through education or through listening to people," said Laura.

If you are affected by any issues raised in this article, help is available at BBC Action Line

RAF Fairford air show cancellation 'devastating'

Has crackdown on crime in city centre worked?

Symptoms can include feeling fearful, anxious or irritable, alongside difficulty concentrating and sleeping.

It can also be accompanied by suicidal thoughts and struggling to bond with your baby.

An NHS spokesperson advised seeking support from your GP, health visitor or midwife if these symptoms persist, in addition to charities such as Mind and PANDAS.

According to the NHS, the condition affects about one in 1,000 new mothers and can include symptoms such as hallucinations, paranoia and depression.

The NHS said it should be treated as a medical emergency.

Laura said her birthing experience with her son Arthur in June 2018 was "traumatic but incredibly quick" after he became "very stressed" in the final stages.

About two months after his arrival, Laura said simple household chores triggered negative thoughts which eventually spiralled into suicidal thoughts.

"I used to think anything I did wasn't good enough," Laura said. "I thought, 'I'm a fraud, they all think I've got something wrong with me'."

Laura and Arthur were admitted to the mother and baby unit at the Barberry - a national centre for mental health in Birmingham.

There, Laura received 10 weeks of specialist inpatient care which she said had made all the difference.

For Jade, 33, from Sherbourne in Dorset, it was a peri-mental health team and an admission to a mother and baby unit in Bournemouth that helped her to get better.

She experienced postpartum psychosis about two weeks after she gave birth to her daughter in December 2020.

Jade said she had spent almost three days in labour before she was induced and she finally delivered her daughter with the help of forceps.

"I didn't realise at the time but, after going through therapy, I realise it was quite a traumatic delivery," she said.

"I experienced tearfulness right away and I think that was trying to process it as I'd wanted a water birth, so it was very different to what I'd envisioned."

Jade sought counselling for her symptoms but was told the NHS was stretched. She was asked if she could seek private help instead.

In March 2021, she was prescribed anti-depressants but she suffered her first psychotic episode two weeks later.

"I was in a completely different reality," she said. "I felt at a loss and things were getting progressively worse.

"I was getting intrusive thoughts which I was too scared to say out loud."

Although she experienced depression following her return home and a relapse of psychosis in January 2024, Jade said the consistent support from her community mental health team and her care co-ordinator had been a "complete lifeline".

Jade said she wanted to share her experience so people knew what the signs of postpartum psychosis were.

"If a mum is acting out of character... and the unusual behaviour isn't right, it's really important that's flagged and is seen as a medical emergency," she said.

After her diagnosis, Laura began to volunteer with the perinatal mental health team "as a way to give back" to the NHS, which she said had carried her through "the lowest time of her life".

She also wrote the book Something to Live For about her experience to raise awareness of postnatal depression.

She said she had received "the most heart-warming messages" from fellow mothers and praise from fathers who credited the book with helping them to understand what their partners may have been going through after birth.

articles.title: Happy Dhanteras 2026: Date, time, puja vidhi, shubh muharat, mantra and muharat to buy gold and silver
articles.summary: The markets are already glowing, jewellers are busy, and homes across the country are being cleaned from top to bottom, because Dhanteras is almost here.
articles.body: The markets are already glowing, jewellers are busy, and homes across the country are being cleaned from top to bottom, because Dhanteras is almost here. It’s the first day of the five-day Diwali festival, and it’s all about welcoming health, wealth and good fortune into your home. This year, Dhanteras falls on Friday, November 6, 2026. On this day, families worship Lord Dhanvantari for good health, Goddess Lakshmi for prosperity and Lord Kubera for financial stability, and many buy gold, silver or a new utensil. Here’s everything you need to know, from the date and muhurat to the puja vidhi and mantras.Dhanteras 2026 date and tithiDhanteras is observed on Trayodashi, the thirteenth day of the waning moon in the month of Kartik. In 2026, the Trayodashi tithi begins at about 10:30 AM on November 6 and ends at around 10:47 AM on November 7. Since the puja is performed in the evening, in Pradosh Kaal, the festival is celebrated on Friday, November 6, when Trayodashi is present at that time.Puja muhurat and Pradosh KaalThe best time for Lakshmi puja on Dhanteras is during Pradosh Kaal, which begins after sunset, particularly during Vrishabha Lagna, which is considered a stable time. For New Delhi, Pradosh Kaal runs from about 5:33 PM to 8:09 PM, and the Dhanteras puja muhurat is from 6:02 PM to 7:57 PM, a window of nearly two hours. Timings differ from city to city, and these are approximate puja muhurats:Delhi: 6:02 PM to 7:57 PMMumbai: 6:35 PM to 8:35 PMBengaluru: 6:25 PM to 8:20 PMKolkata: 5:28 PM to 7:26 PMAhmedabad: 6:30 PM to 8:28 PMPune: 6:32 PM to 8:31 PMChennai: 6:14 PM to 8:10 PMMuhurat to buy gold and silverGold, silver and utensils can be bought any time after the Trayodashi tithi begins on November 6, and many people consider the entire day auspicious. If you’d like to pick a specific window, the Pradosh and Vrishabha Kaal period in the evening is widely considered the best. Based on the Choghadiya for Delhi, other good windows are the Shubh muhurat from 12:04 PM to 1:26 PM, Char from 4:10 PM to 5:32 PM and Labh from 8:48 PM to 10:27 PM. Check your local panchang for your city.What to buy, and what to avoidTraditionally, people buy gold or silver coins, jewellery, and brass, copper or steel utensils. A new broom and whole coriander seeds are also considered auspicious. A small silver coin or a single new utensil is perfectly fine, so there’s no need to stretch your budget. Many families avoid buying iron items and sharp objects like knives and scissors on this day, and they bring home utensils filled with something, rather than empty. Customs vary by region, so follow your family tradition.Dhanteras puja vidhi at homeA simple puja at home is enough. Here’s a step-by-step guide:Clean your home, decorate the entrance with rangoli and hang a mango leaf toran on the main door.Take a bath before the puja and wear clean clothes.Place a chowki with a clean red or yellow cloth, and set up images or idols of Ganesha, Dhanvantari, Lakshmi and Kubera.Light a ghee diya and incense, and begin by worshipping Lord Ganesha.Worship Lord Dhanvantari, followed by Goddess Lakshmi and Lord Kubera, offering flowers, haldi, kumkum, akshat, sweets and fruits.Place your newly bought gold, silver coins or utensils on the chowki and offer prayers.Perform aarti, and then share the prasad with family.Mantras to chantYou can chant these during the puja, and you can use the shorter versions if you prefer.Lord Dhanvantari: “Om Dhanvantaraye Namah”Goddess Lakshmi: “Om Shreem Hreem Shreem Kamale Kamalalaye Prasida Prasida Om Shreem Hreem Shreem Mahalakshmyai Namah”Lord Kubera: “Om Yakshaya Kuberaya Vaishravanaya Dhanadhanyadhipataye Dhanadhanyasamriddhim Me Dehi Dapaya Swaha”Yama Deepam: the lamp at the doorAfter the puja, at dusk, a special lamp called the Yama Deepam is lit in honour of Yama, the god of death, to protect the family. Take a clay lamp filled with mustard oil, with four wicks, and place it outside the main door, facing south. Light it within Pradosh Kaal, ideally before 8:09 PM in Delhi. Many families also light thirteen small diyas around the house.A festival about more than goldAt its heart, Dhanteras isn’t just about buying something shiny. It’s a reminder that health is the first wealth, and that gratitude brings prosperity. Whether you buy a gold coin, a steel vessel or nothing at all, a clean home, a lit lamp and a thankful heart are a lovely way to begin Diwali. Happy Dhanteras to you and your family.Disclaimer:This article is intended for general informational purposes only. Muhurat timings are based on published panchang data and can vary by city, so please check a local panchang or consult your family priest. Rituals and customs differ by region and tradition. Take care when using lamps, diyas and incense, and keep them away from curtains, decorations and children. Buy gold and silver from trusted, hallmarked sellers and within your budget.Get the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates. Download the TOI App.

New aerial images have been released which show the devastating impact of a wildfire.

It is three months since a blaze ravaged Dunwich Heath in Suffolk, which the National Trust has warned faces "a long recovery".

More than 104 hectares (257 acres) of heathland were destroyed, and recent monitoring has shown "significant impacts" on the health of the soil.

"The destruction has been so complete that [although] we will see some early regrowth, a full recovery is likely to take decades," said the trust's Russell Clement.

He added: "This is the beginning of a very long journey, but after three challenging months, we are looking to the future with hope."

Clement, the charity's general manager for Suffolk and Essex Coast, thanked the public after thousands of people donated to an emergency fundraiser .

More than £500,000 is being used to fund two years of repair and recovery work at the heath, which is not expected to fully reopen for "many months".

Since August, teams have been monitoring cliff stability and burn severity, and testing soil, water, and ash.

Some areas of soil lost 82% of their organic matter, making it harder to store water and more vulnerable to drought, the trust said.

Clement added: "The intensity of the blaze was absolutely astounding".

"It's not only things above the ground that have burned: tree roots have burned down to a metre below ground level.

"What that means is the entire seed bank and topsoil has been sterilised and lost," he said.

Experts have also inspected "badly burned" trees which were left standing.

The trust's coast and countryside manager, Matt Wilson, said: "We don't yet know the full impact on the trees."

"Some were felled while the fire was burning, to help with access, but many of those still standing will have been weakened and may not survive the winter storms.

"We need to make sure the site is safe for visitors," he added.

The charity, which owns and manages Dunwich Heath, said it hoped to "retain as many trees as possible" but "any found to be a risk will need to be removed".

As well as the trees, unstable terrain, high ground temperatures and dust pollution are also concerns.

"Even for us that know the site really well - it's really difficult to navigate.

"Most of those visual markers, and the places that people think they know, do not look the same currently," said Wilson.

Clement said they were seeing "really positive signs for wildlife".

"One thing we can be grateful for is we didn't find a lot of animal remains, so we know that most of the fauna will have escaped the blaze."

Large parts of RSPB Minsmere were also damaged during the wildfire. How it started is still not known .

Wilson added: "The biggest worry for me is the loss of vegetation and that organic layer on the soil.

"There is nothing here for the wildlife that would normally call it home to return to."

He said they were "seeing some signs of recovery", but it was on a "very, very small scale".

For Wilson and his colleagues, the sense of loss is immense.

"Growing up, I came here as a child. My children came here on family holidays.

"It's always been part and parcel of my life, even before working for the National Trust.

"My heart drops every time I drive in through the entrance," he said.

"It was a horrific, emotional experience for everyone involved. I have some volunteers and staff who've worked literally 20 to 30 years in this landscape."

Now they are focusing all their efforts on slowly restoring that landscape.

"There are things we can do, and nature often has the solution.

"It's making it wetter where we can, improving the mosaic, looking at the diversity of the species," he said.

"We will make the landscape more resilient and better able to adapt to the new climate that it's finding itself in," he added.
